topics.name: P1 Q5: Descriptive or narrative writing

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel set on a remote stretch of coast.

The storm arrived at Carrick Head three hours before anyone expected it. Elsie Marr was halfway up the iron staircase of the lighthouse, a tin of paraffin in each hand, when the first gust struck the tower and the whole building seemed to inhale.

Below her, the sea was no longer a sea. It was a grey animal, heaving and clawing at the rocks, flinging white spit high against the windows. Rain came sideways. It hissed on the glass like fat in a pan.

Read again the first two paragraphs of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about the storm and the sea.
questions.answer: Any four from: the storm arrived three hours earlier than expected; a gust struck the lighthouse tower; the sea was grey; the sea was heaving / clawing at the rocks; it flung white spray (spit) high against the windows; the rain came sideways; the rain hissed on the glass.
ms: 1 mark: the storm arrived three hours earlier than anyone expected
1 mark: the sea was grey / heaving / clawing at the rocks
1 mark: it threw white spray high against the windows
1 mark: the rain came sideways / hissed on the glass

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel about a young woman arriving in London.

Amara stepped off the night coach into a morning that smelled of diesel and warm bread. Victoria Coach Station was already awake. Pigeons strutted between suitcases. A man in an orange vest swept the same patch of pavement over and over, as if he were trying to erase it.

Read again the first paragraph of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about Victoria Coach Station.
questions.answer: Any four from: it smelled of diesel; it smelled of warm bread; it was already awake / busy in the morning; pigeons strutted between the suitcases; there were suitcases around; a man in an orange vest was sweeping the pavement; he swept the same patch over and over.
ms: 1 mark: it smelled of diesel (and/or warm bread; allow as two separate points)
1 mark: it was already busy / awake
1 mark: there were pigeons strutting between suitcases
1 mark: a man in an orange vest was sweeping (the same patch repeatedly)

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a short story set in a small town.

Mr Abernethy's shop had not changed in forty years, and neither, it seemed, had Mr Abernethy. He sat behind the counter on the same high stool, in the same moss-green cardigan, with the same jeweller's glass screwed into his left eye.

Around him, the clocks kept talking. There were dozens of them: carriage clocks and cuckoo clocks, a grandfather clock as tall and solemn as a judge, a brass ship's clock that had once crossed the Atlantic. Each one ticked at a slightly different pace, so that the room was filled with a soft, endless argument about what time it really was.

Read again the first two paragraphs of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about Mr Abernethy and his shop.
questions.answer: Any four from: the shop had not changed in forty years; Mr Abernethy had not seemed to change either; he sat behind the counter on a high stool; he wore a moss-green cardigan; he had a jeweller's glass in his left eye; there were dozens of clocks; there was a grandfather clock / a ship's clock that had crossed the Atlantic / carriage and cuckoo clocks; the clocks ticked at slightly different speeds.
ms: 1 mark: the shop / Mr Abernethy had not changed in forty years
1 mark: he sat on a high stool behind the counter / wore a moss-green cardigan
1 mark: he had a jeweller's glass in his left eye
1 mark: the shop held dozens of clocks of different kinds, ticking at different paces

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel set on a winter train journey.

Outside, the world had been erased. Fields, fences, the distant line of trees: all of it smoothed into one white page. Only the telegraph poles remained, black and crooked, marching away into the blizzard like a line of mourners.

Inside the carriage, the lights flickered. A baby began to cry. The businessman opposite Daniel checked his watch, tapped it, checked it again, as though time itself might be persuaded to hurry.

Read again this part of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about what Daniel can see and hear around him.
questions.answer: Any four from: the fields, fences and trees were covered in white; the telegraph poles were still visible; the poles were black and crooked; it was a blizzard; the lights in the carriage flickered; a baby began to cry; the businessman opposite kept checking and tapping his watch.
ms: 1 mark: everything outside (fields, fences, trees) was covered / smoothed white
1 mark: black, crooked telegraph poles stretched away
1 mark: the carriage lights flickered
1 mark: a baby cried / the businessman checked and tapped his watch

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text. Allow 'snow was falling' or 'there was a blizzard'.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel set in a village during a drought.

Every morning, before the heat rose, Nadia walked to the well with two plastic jerrycans. The path was three kilometres long. She knew every stone on it. She knew the thorn bush that snagged her sleeve, the dead acacia where the vultures waited, the place where the ground dipped and the air went suddenly cooler, as though remembering something.

Read again this part of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about Nadia's walk to the well.
questions.answer: Any four from: she walks every morning; she goes before the heat rises; she carries two plastic jerrycans; the path is three kilometres long; she knows every stone; a thorn bush snags her sleeve; there is a dead acacia tree where vultures wait; there is a dip where the air goes cooler.
ms: 1 mark: she goes every morning, before the heat rises
1 mark: she carries two plastic jerrycans
1 mark: the path is three kilometres long / she knows every stone
1 mark: she passes a thorn bush, a dead acacia with vultures, or a cooler dip in the ground

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel set on a London housing estate.

The roof of Hartley Tower was the only place where Kieran could hear himself think.

Twenty-two floors below, the estate went about its evening business. Car alarms. A dog that never stopped barking. Somebody's music thumping out of an open window, the bass so heavy it seemed to come up through the concrete and into his trainers. From up here it all sounded small, like a radio left on in another room.

Read again the first two paragraphs of the source.

List four things from this part of the source about the estate below Kieran.
questions.answer: Any four from: it is twenty-two floors below; car alarms go off; a dog never stops barking; music thumps out of an open window; the bass is so heavy it comes up through the concrete; from the roof it all sounds small.
ms: 1 mark: it is twenty-two floors below the roof
1 mark: there are car alarms / a dog that never stops barking
1 mark: loud music thumps from an open window (heavy bass)
1 mark: from the roof the noise sounds small, like a radio in another room

Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. Points must be true and taken from the named part of the source only. Allow direct quotation or paraphrase. Do not accept points from outside the named paragraphs, or inferences that are not supported by the text.
questions.tip: Five minutes, four short points, no analysis. Stay inside the paragraphs named: anything from outside them scores zero even if it is true.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel about a young woman arriving in London.

She had one bag, one phone with eleven per cent battery, and one address written in her aunt's careful capitals on the back of an envelope. She had folded the envelope so many times on the journey that the words had begun to wear thin along the creases.

Which of these is NOT something we learn about the young woman in this paragraph?
options: She has her aunt's address on an envelope
She has a return ticket home
Her phone battery is at eleven per cent
ms: The paragraph mentions the bag, the battery and the envelope. A return ticket is never mentioned, so it cannot be used.
questions.tip: Q1 only rewards what is actually in the named lines. Do not invent or assume details.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 1

Source: the opening of a novel set on a winter train journey.

Inside the carriage, the lights flickered. A baby began to cry. The businessman opposite Daniel checked his watch, tapped it, checked it again, as though time itself might be persuaded to hurry.

'Ladies and gentlemen,' crackled the speaker, 'we apologise for the delay.' Then the voice stopped, mid-breath, and did not return.

A student lists four things about the carriage. Which of their points would NOT get a mark?
options: The speaker apologised for the delay
The passengers were terrified of the shape outside
ms: No shape outside and no fear among the passengers are mentioned anywhere in this part of the text. The point is invented, so it cannot earn a mark. The other three are stated directly.
questions.tip: Q1 tests explicit information. A guess about feelings is not a 'thing from the text'.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel set on a remote stretch of coast.

The storm arrived at Carrick Head three hours before anyone expected it. Elsie Marr was halfway up the iron staircase of the lighthouse, a tin of paraffin in each hand, when the first gust struck the tower and the whole building seemed to inhale.

Below her, the sea was no longer a sea. It was a grey animal, heaving and clawing at the rocks, flinging white spit high against the windows. Rain came sideways. It hissed on the glass like fat in a pan.

How does the writer use language here to describe the storm?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The writer presents the storm as a living predator. The metaphor 'grey animal' turns the sea into a beast, and the violent verbs 'heaving and clawing' suggest something both exhausted and vicious, attacking the rocks as if trying to tear them apart. 'Spit' is deliberately disgusting: the spray becomes the saliva of a snarling creature. Even the building reacts, as personification makes it 'inhale', as if holding its breath in fear. The short sentence 'Rain came sideways.' is blunt and abrupt, mirroring the sudden force of the weather, and the simile 'like fat in a pan' takes a homely kitchen sound and makes it threatening, hinting at heat, danger and something about to burn.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: metaphor 'grey animal' presents the sea as a living predator; verbs 'heaving and clawing' (present participles) suggest relentless, violent movement; 'spit' has connotations of aggression and disgust; personification 'the whole building seemed to inhale' suggests fear / bracing for impact; the short simple sentence 'Rain came sideways.' creates abruptness and shock; the simile 'like fat in a pan' uses a domestic sound to suggest danger and spitting heat; the opening clause 'three hours before anyone expected it' suggests unpredictability.
questions.tip: Zoom in on single words and say what they suggest. A technique name with no effect earns almost nothing; 'the verb clawing suggests...' earns marks.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel about a young woman arriving in London.

London did not look at her. That was the first thing she noticed. In Accra, people looked. Here, faces slid past like coins dropped into a slot, quick and silver and gone. A woman in a camel coat talked into the air. A boy on a scooter threaded through the crowd without once lifting his eyes from the ground.

Amara tightened her grip on the bag strap. Above her, the sky was the colour of dishwater, low and heavy, pressing down on the rooftops.

How does the writer use language here to describe London and how Amara feels about it?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The writer makes London seem cold and indifferent. The short sentence 'London did not look at her' personifies the city as someone deliberately ignoring her, which makes her loneliness feel personal. The simile 'faces slid past like coins dropped into a slot' is impersonal and transactional: people become objects, and the triplet 'quick and silver and gone' uses polysyndeton to speed the sentence up, as if the faces vanish before she can register them. The sky is 'the colour of dishwater', a dull, dirty image of pathetic fallacy, and the verb 'pressing' suggests weight and claustrophobia, reflecting how overwhelmed she feels. Her physical reaction, 'tightened her grip', shows her anxiety without stating it.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: personification 'London did not look at her' suggests coldness and rejection; contrast with 'In Accra, people looked' emphasises isolation; simile 'like coins dropped into a slot' dehumanises the crowd; polysyndeton 'quick and silver and gone' creates speed and transience; 'talked into the air' suggests people are disconnected from each other; pathetic fallacy 'the colour of dishwater' creates dullness; 'low and heavy, pressing down' suggests a crushing, claustrophobic atmosphere; 'tightened her grip' implies anxiety.
questions.tip: Zoom in on single words and say what they suggest. A technique name with no effect earns almost nothing; 'the verb clawing suggests...' earns marks.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a short story set in a small town.

Around him, the clocks kept talking. There were dozens of them: carriage clocks and cuckoo clocks, a grandfather clock as tall and solemn as a judge, a brass ship's clock that had once crossed the Atlantic. Each one ticked at a slightly different pace, so that the room was filled with a soft, endless argument about what time it really was.

Nobody came in any more. The high street had emptied, shop by shop, like teeth falling from a mouth. The bakery was a phone repair stall now. The bookshop was boarded up, its window a patchwork of faded posters.

How does the writer use language here to describe the shop and the high street?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The writer contrasts the busy, almost human life of the shop with the decay outside. The clocks 'kept talking', personification that fills the room with company, and the simile 'as tall and solemn as a judge' gives the grandfather clock authority, as if time itself sits in judgement. The phrase 'a soft, endless argument about what time it really was' is gently comic but also suggests a place where time is uncertain and slightly stuck. Outside, the simile 'like teeth falling from a mouth' is grotesque: the high street is an ageing body, and the loss is painful, gradual and permanent. The noun 'patchwork' suggests something pieced together from scraps, and 'faded' links to neglect, so the town feels forgotten.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: listing of clocks ('carriage clocks and cuckoo clocks...') creates abundance; personification 'kept talking' and 'argument' makes the clocks companions; simile 'solemn as a judge' suggests authority and seriousness; 'soft, endless argument' suggests confusion about time and the shop being out of step with the world; simile 'like teeth falling from a mouth' presents decline as ageing and decay; contrast 'The bakery was a phone repair stall now' shows change; 'boarded up', 'faded' build a semantic field of abandonment. Level 4 answers may link the time imagery to Mr Abernethy being left behind by the modern world.
questions.tip: The best answers notice how two images work together (the lively shop against the dying street) rather than treating each quotation in isolation.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel set on a winter train journey.

For a long minute, nobody spoke. The engine's hum died to a whisper, then to nothing, and the silence that followed was so complete that Daniel could hear the snow. It fell against the window with a sound like someone breathing out.

Outside, the world had been erased. Fields, fences, the distant line of trees: all of it smoothed into one white page. Only the telegraph poles remained, black and crooked, marching away into the blizzard like a line of mourners.

How does the writer use language here to describe the silence and the snow?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The writer creates an eerie, deathly stillness. The silence is 'so complete that Daniel could hear the snow', a paradox that makes the quiet almost unnatural, and the simile 'like someone breathing out' hints at an unseen presence close to the window. The verb 'erased' and the metaphor 'one white page' suggest the landscape has been wiped clean, leaving Daniel cut off from the normal world. The telegraph poles are 'black and crooked', a stark colour contrast, and the simile 'like a line of mourners' introduces a semantic field of death, foreshadowing that something sinister is coming.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: the gradual fading 'to a whisper, then to nothing' (a sentence that slows down) builds tension; 'could hear the snow' is unexpected and emphasises total silence; simile 'like someone breathing out' suggests a human presence and creates unease; 'erased' and 'one white page' suggest the world has been wiped out, isolation; listing 'Fields, fences, the distant line of trees' followed by a colon emphasises how much has disappeared; 'black and crooked' contrasts with white and suggests something wrong or twisted; simile 'line of mourners' links to death and funerals and foreshadows danger.
questions.tip: Zoom in on single words and say what they suggest. A technique name with no effect earns almost nothing; 'the verb clawing suggests...' earns marks.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel set in a village during a drought.

By August, the river had become a rumour.

The old people of Kesra still talked about it as if it were there, pointing down the valley to where it used to run, wide and brown and generous. But the children had never seen it. To them, the riverbed was simply a road of cracked clay, split into a thousand pale tiles that crunched underfoot like broken plates.

How does the writer use language here to describe the effects of the drought?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The opening metaphor 'the river had become a rumour' is startling: something once solid and life-giving now exists only in words, so the drought feels total. The alliteration of 'river' and 'rumour' makes the line memorable and slightly mournful. The old people remember it as 'wide and brown and generous', where polysyndeton slows the sentence into a loving list and 'generous' personifies the river as a giver, making its absence feel like a loss of kindness. The present is brutal by contrast: the riverbed is 'a road of cracked clay', the harsh alliterative 'c' sounds suggesting dryness, and the simile 'like broken plates' links the land to a damaged home, implying the community itself is breaking.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: metaphor 'become a rumour' suggests the river has disappeared so long it is almost myth; alliteration 'river / rumour' and 'cracked clay'; polysyndeton 'wide and brown and generous' creates a nostalgic, abundant tone; personification 'generous'; contrast between the old people's memories and the children's experience shows the drought has lasted a generation; 'split into a thousand pale tiles' suggests fragmentation, with hyperbole emphasising scale; onomatopoeic 'crunched' and simile 'like broken plates' suggest destruction of domestic life.
questions.tip: For level 4, explore layers: 'generous' is not just personification, it suggests the river was a giver and its loss is almost a betrayal.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel set on a London housing estate.

Twenty-two floors below, the estate went about its evening business. Car alarms. A dog that never stopped barking. Somebody's music thumping out of an open window, the bass so heavy it seemed to come up through the concrete and into his trainers. From up here it all sounded small, like a radio left on in another room.

He sat with his back against the water tank, knees pulled up, and watched the city switch itself on. One by one the windows lit: yellow, white, the cold blue flicker of televisions. Further out, the towers of the City glittered like a mouthful of gold teeth.

How does the writer use language here to describe the view from the roof?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The writer uses noise and light to show Kieran's distance from the world below. The fragments 'Car alarms. A dog that never stopped barking.' read like a list of irritations, but from the roof 'it all sounded small, like a radio left on in another room', a simile that suggests the noise no longer has power over him. The personification 'watched the city switch itself on' makes London feel alive and mechanical at once. Colours build a vivid picture, 'yellow, white, the cold blue flicker of televisions', and the simile 'like a mouthful of gold teeth' suggests wealth that is glamorous but slightly threatening, as if the City is grinning at him.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: minor sentences / fragments 'Car alarms.' list noise and create a choppy rhythm; 'thumping' and 'so heavy it seemed to come up through the concrete' show how intrusive noise is; simile 'like a radio left on in another room' shows distance and escape; personification 'switch itself on'; list of colours; 'cold blue flicker' suggests isolation; simile 'mouthful of gold teeth' suggests wealth, flashiness or menace, contrasting with the estate.
questions.tip: Zoom in on single words and say what they suggest. A technique name with no effect earns almost nothing; 'the verb clawing suggests...' earns marks.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2

Look in detail at this extract from the source.

Source: from the opening of a novel set on a remote stretch of coast.

At the top, the lamp room was cold and smelled of oil and rust. The great lens sat in its cradle, waiting, patient as a sleeping eye. Elsie set down the tins, struck a match and cupped it against the draught.

It went out.

She struck another. Somewhere out in that howling dark, she knew, a boat was trying to find its way home.

How does the writer use language here to describe the lamp room and Elsie's situation?

You could include the writer's choice of:
- words and phrases
- language features and techniques
- sentence forms.
questions.answer: The lamp room is presented as cold and neglected: 'smelled of oil and rust' uses smell to suggest age and decay. The simile 'patient as a sleeping eye' personifies the lens, making it seem alive and watchful, and links to the lighthouse's job of seeing ships. The one-sentence paragraph 'It went out.' is blunt and final; its shortness mirrors the sudden death of the flame and builds tension. The phrase 'that howling dark' gives the darkness a voice, making it a hostile force, while 'trying to find its way home' adds emotional stakes, as 'home' suggests safety and people who are waiting.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight, often exploring more than one layer of meaning in a single word or image; quotations are short, precise and well chosen; subject terminology is sophisticated and always used to support a point about effect, never just to label.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): explains the effects of language clearly; uses a relevant range of quotations; subject terminology is accurate and helps the explanation.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): comments on language are simple or partly relevant; quotations may be long or loosely linked; terminology is attempted but not always accurate.

Valid points include: sensory language 'cold and smelled of oil and rust'; simile 'patient as a sleeping eye' personifies the lens; verbs 'struck' and 'cupped' show her care and urgency; the short simple sentence 'It went out.' creates tension and shock; repetition 'She struck another' shows determination; 'howling dark' personifies the darkness as an animal or a crying voice; 'find its way home' creates pathos.
questions.tip: Zoom in on single words and say what they suggest. A technique name with no effect earns almost nothing; 'the verb clawing suggests...' earns marks.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2: a student is writing about this quotation from a short story.

'The high street had emptied, shop by shop, like teeth falling from a mouth.'

Which sentence from their answer would be credited most highly?
options: The writer uses a simile, 'like teeth falling from a mouth', which is very effective and makes the reader want to read on.
The simile compares the high street to a mouth losing teeth, suggesting decay that is gradual and painful, as if the town is ageing and cannot grow back what it has lost.
The writer uses a metaphor to show the high street is empty.
This tells us that lots of shops have closed down on the high street over the years.
ms: Option B identifies the technique accurately and explores what the image suggests (decay, pain, permanence). A is generic, C mislabels the technique, D only retells the content.
questions.tip: Avoid empty phrases like 'makes the reader want to read on'. Say what the specific image suggests.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 2: 'The sea was no longer a sea. It was a grey animal, heaving and clawing at the rocks.'

Which comment best analyses the writer's sentence forms here?
options: The writer uses a long sentence to describe the sea.

The short opening sentence sets up a sudden transformation, and the second sentence delivers it as a metaphor, so the structure mirrors the sea changing from something familiar into something monstrous.
The writer uses commas to separate the words.
The writer uses a rhetorical question to make the reader think about the sea.
ms: B explains how the pairing of sentences creates an effect linked to meaning. A and C describe rather than analyse; D is inaccurate (there is no question).
questions.tip: Sentence forms count in Q2: always link length or type to an effect on meaning or pace.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a novel set on a remote stretch of coast.

The storm arrived at Carrick Head three hours before anyone expected it. Elsie Marr was halfway up the iron staircase of the lighthouse, a tin of paraffin in each hand, when the first gust struck the tower and the whole building seemed to inhale.

Below her, the sea was no longer a sea. It was a grey animal, heaving and clawing at the rocks, flinging white spit high against the windows. Rain came sideways. It hissed on the glass like fat in a pan.

She climbed on. One hundred and twelve steps. She had counted them every night for nine years, ever since her father's hands had grown too stiff to grip the rail, and tonight she counted them again, aloud, because the sound of her own voice was the only thing in the tower that was not shaking.

At the top, the lamp room was cold and smelled of oil and rust. The great lens sat in its cradle, waiting, patient as a sleeping eye. Elsie set down the tins, struck a match and cupped it against the draught.

It went out.

She struck another. Somewhere out in that howling dark, she knew, a boat was trying to find its way home.

You now need to think about the whole of the source.

This text is from the opening of a novel.

How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?

You could write about:
- what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning of the source
- how and why the writer changes this focus as the source develops

Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a novel about a young woman arriving in London.

Amara stepped off the night coach into a morning that smelled of diesel and warm bread. Victoria Coach Station was already awake. Pigeons strutted between suitcases. A man in an orange vest swept the same patch of pavement over and over, as if he were trying to erase it.

She had one bag, one phone with eleven per cent battery, and one address written in her aunt's careful capitals on the back of an envelope. She had folded the envelope so many times on the journey that the words had begun to wear thin along the creases.

London did not look at her. That was the first thing she noticed. In Accra, people looked. Here, faces slid past like coins dropped into a slot, quick and silver and gone. A woman in a camel coat talked into the air. A boy on a scooter threaded through the crowd without once lifting his eyes from the ground.

Amara tightened her grip on the bag strap. Above her, the sky was the colour of dishwater, low and heavy, pressing down on the rooftops.

Then, from somewhere behind the ticket office, someone began to play a steel pan. The notes rose, bright and round, and for a moment the whole grey morning seemed to tilt towards the sun.

Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a short story set in a small town.

Mr Abernethy's shop had not changed in forty years, and neither, it seemed, had Mr Abernethy. He sat behind the counter on the same high stool, in the same moss-green cardigan, with the same jeweller's glass screwed into his left eye.

Around him, the clocks kept talking. There were dozens of them: carriage clocks and cuckoo clocks, a grandfather clock as tall and solemn as a judge, a brass ship's clock that had once crossed the Atlantic. Each one ticked at a slightly different pace, so that the room was filled with a soft, endless argument about what time it really was.

Nobody came in any more. The high street had emptied, shop by shop, like teeth falling from a mouth. The bakery was a phone repair stall now. The bookshop was boarded up, its window a patchwork of faded posters.

But on Tuesday afternoon, at exactly four o'clock, the bell above the door rang.

Mr Abernethy did not look up at first. He was used to the wind playing tricks. Then a small voice said, 'Excuse me. Can you fix time?'

He lowered the glass. A girl of about eight stood on the mat, holding out a broken wristwatch in both hands as if it were a wounded bird.

questions.answer: The writer begins with stillness: the repetition of 'same' establishes a man and a shop frozen in time. The focus widens from Mr Abernethy to the clocks around him, then further out to the dying high street, so the reader understands that the world has moved on while he has not. This slow, static opening makes the one-line paragraph 'But on Tuesday afternoon, at exactly four o'clock, the bell above the door rang.' a sharp turning point: 'But' signals disruption, and the precise time is ironic in a shop full of disagreeing clocks. The pace then slows again as he delays looking up, building anticipation. The story's first dialogue, 'Can you fix time?', introduces a new character and a central mystery, and the closing image of the girl holding the watch 'as if it were a wounded bird' ends on a question the reader wants answered.

Valid points include: static opening and repetition establish routine; widening focus from man to shop to high street; contrast between the timeless shop and the changing town; one-line paragraph beginning 'But' marks the inciting incident; precise time creates irony; delay before he looks up builds tension; introduction of dialogue and a new character; ending on the girl and the watch creates a hook. Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a novel set on a winter train journey.

The train stopped somewhere between two stations that no longer mattered.

For a long minute, nobody spoke. The engine's hum died to a whisper, then to nothing, and the silence that followed was so complete that Daniel could hear the snow. It fell against the window with a sound like someone breathing out.

Outside, the world had been erased. Fields, fences, the distant line of trees: all of it smoothed into one white page. Only the telegraph poles remained, black and crooked, marching away into the blizzard like a line of mourners.

Inside the carriage, the lights flickered. A baby began to cry. The businessman opposite Daniel checked his watch, tapped it, checked it again, as though time itself might be persuaded to hurry.

'Ladies and gentlemen,' crackled the speaker, 'we apologise for the delay.' Then the voice stopped, mid-breath, and did not return.

Daniel pressed his forehead to the glass. It was so cold it burned. Far off, beyond the last pole, something moved: a dark shape, upright, walking slowly through the snow towards the train.

It did not seem to be leaving any footprints.

Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a novel set in a village during a drought.

By August, the river had become a rumour.

The old people of Kesra still talked about it as if it were there, pointing down the valley to where it used to run, wide and brown and generous. But the children had never seen it. To them, the riverbed was simply a road of cracked clay, split into a thousand pale tiles that crunched underfoot like broken plates.

Every morning, before the heat rose, Nadia walked to the well with two plastic jerrycans. The path was three kilometres long. She knew every stone on it. She knew the thorn bush that snagged her sleeve, the dead acacia where the vultures waited, the place where the ground dipped and the air went suddenly cooler, as though remembering something.

The well was deeper every week. Or perhaps the water was shallower. It came to the same thing.

Today, when she lowered the bucket, she heard it knock against stone. Not splash. Knock.

She stood very still. The sun had cleared the hills now and was pressing on the back of her neck like a hot hand. Behind her, in the village, a goat bleated. Ahead of her, the dark mouth of the well said nothing at all.

Paper 1 Question 3

Source: the opening of a novel set on a London housing estate.

The roof of Hartley Tower was the only place where Kieran could hear himself think.

Twenty-two floors below, the estate went about its evening business. Car alarms. A dog that never stopped barking. Somebody's music thumping out of an open window, the bass so heavy it seemed to come up through the concrete and into his trainers. From up here it all sounded small, like a radio left on in another room.

He sat with his back against the water tank, knees pulled up, and watched the city switch itself on. One by one the windows lit: yellow, white, the cold blue flicker of televisions. Further out, the towers of the City glittered like a mouthful of gold teeth.

His mum thought he was at Dev's. Dev thought he was at home. Nobody knew about the roof, and that was the point.

He took the letter out of his pocket. He had read it so many times that he could have recited it, but he unfolded it anyway, smoothing it flat against his knee. The paper was thin. The words were not.

We are pleased to offer you a place.

He looked out at the lights, and for the first time in his life, they looked like they were waiting for him.

A shift in focus from the setting to a character

questions.tip: If you could only spot it by zooming in on a single word, it is probably language, not structure.

questions.q: In a lighthouse story, the line 'It went out.' is placed as a paragraph on its own, straight after Elsie strikes a match. What is the main structural effect?
options: It isolates a moment of failure, slowing the pace and building tension
ms: A one-line paragraph isolates a moment and forces the reader to pause, here emphasising that the flame has failed at the worst moment.
questions.tip: Name the feature (one-line paragraph) and its effect (pace, emphasis, tension). Both are needed.

questions.q: A novel opens with a boy looking at city lights from a roof, feeling distant from them. It ends with the same lights, which now 'looked like they were waiting for him'. Which term best describes this structure?

Paper 1 Question 4

Source: the opening of a novel set on a remote stretch of coast.

The storm arrived at Carrick Head three hours before anyone expected it. Elsie Marr was halfway up the iron staircase of the lighthouse, a tin of paraffin in each hand, when the first gust struck the tower and the whole building seemed to inhale.

Below her, the sea was no longer a sea. It was a grey animal, heaving and clawing at the rocks, flinging white spit high against the windows. Rain came sideways. It hissed on the glass like fat in a pan.

She climbed on. One hundred and twelve steps. She had counted them every night for nine years, ever since her father's hands had grown too stiff to grip the rail, and tonight she counted them again, aloud, because the sound of her own voice was the only thing in the tower that was not shaking.

At the top, the lamp room was cold and smelled of oil and rust. The great lens sat in its cradle, waiting, patient as a sleeping eye. Elsie set down the tins, struck a match and cupped it against the draught.

It went out.

She struck another. Somewhere out in that howling dark, she knew, a boat was trying to find its way home.

Focus this part of your answer on the second half of the source, from 'She climbed on.' to the end.

A student said, 'In this part of the story, the writer makes Elsie seem brave and determined, but also very alone.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
- consider your own impressions of Elsie
- evaluate how the writer creates these impressions
- support your response with references to the text.
questions.answer: I largely agree, although the writer suggests her loneliness is what drives her bravery. Her determination is clear from the short, insistent 'She climbed on.' and the precise 'One hundred and twelve steps', which shows a disciplined, almost ritual commitment. The detail that she counts 'aloud, because the sound of her own voice was the only thing in the tower that was not shaking' is the most powerful evidence: it shows fear, but also courage in controlling that fear. Her isolation is stressed by the backstory of her father's stiff hands; she has carried this duty alone 'for nine years'. When 'It went out.' is followed immediately by 'She struck another', the juxtaposition is convincing proof of resilience. However, the final paragraph widens her loneliness into connection: thinking of the boat 'trying to find its way home' suggests she is not simply alone but responsible for others, which makes her bravery selfless rather than stubborn.
ms: Level 4 (16-20 marks): critical, detailed and convincing evaluation of the statement; shows perceptive understanding of the writer's methods and how they create effects; a judicious range of quotations; evaluates (agrees, partly agrees, qualifies) rather than just describes.
Level 3 (11-15 marks): clear and relevant evaluation of the statement; clear understanding of the writer's methods; a relevant range of quotations; clear comments on effects on the reader.
Level 2 and below (1-10 marks): some or simple evaluation; some reference to methods; quotations sometimes relevant; may retell the story.

Valid points include: 'She climbed on.' (short sentence, determination); counting steps 'aloud' shows controlled fear; 'only thing in the tower that was not shaking' shows isolation and courage; backstory of father's hands shows burden and duty; lamp room 'cold' reinforces loneliness; 'It went out.' / 'She struck another.' juxtaposition shows resilience; the boat shows her selflessness and the stakes. Higher answers will qualify the statement (e.g. her isolation is physical, but emotionally she is connected to the people at sea).
questions.tip: Q4 is worth 20 marks: spend 20 minutes. Take a clear stance on the statement, use 'the writer' throughout, and judge HOW WELL the methods work, not just what they are.

The pathetic fallacy of a sky 'the colour of dishwater... pressing down' reinforces her sense of being overwhelmed. However, the final paragraph overturns this. The steel pan's notes are 'bright and round', and 'the whole grey morning seemed to tilt towards the sun', which suggests warmth and familiarity, perhaps a reminder of home. Mr Abernethy's assumption that it is 'the wind playing tricks' shows how used he is to loneliness, which makes the girl's voice more surprising. Her question, 'Can you fix time?', is the heart of the magic: a child's misunderstanding that also hints at something fairy-tale-like, as if the shop really can. The simile 'as if it were a wounded bird' shows her tenderness and suggests something fragile that could be healed, which is a hopeful image. It did not seem to be leaving any footprints.

Focus this part of your answer on the second half of the source, from 'Inside the carriage, the lights flickered.' to the end.

A student said, 'The writer builds tension so that by the end, the reader feels genuinely frightened.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
- consider your own impressions of the tension in this part of the story
- evaluate how the writer creates these impressions
- support your response with references to the text.
questions.answer: I agree. The writer builds tension through a gradual removal of comfort. The flickering lights and the crying baby create small but growing unease, and the businessman who 'checked his watch, tapped it, checked it again' shows that even adults are losing control; the repetition makes time feel stuck. The interrupted announcement is especially effective: the reassuring cliché 'we apologise for the delay' stops 'mid-breath' and 'did not return', which is far more frightening than any explanation. Daniel's forehead against glass 'so cold it burned' is a paradox that makes the physical setting hostile. The writer then narrows our focus to 'something' moving, a deliberately vague pronoun that lets the reader imagine the worst. The final one-sentence paragraph, 'It did not seem to be leaving any footprints', delivers a chilling, supernatural revelation in calm, plain language, which makes it more unsettling. The reader is left frightened precisely because nothing is explained.
ms: Level 4 (16-20 marks): critical, detailed and convincing evaluation of the statement; shows perceptive understanding of the writer's methods and how they create effects; a judicious range of quotations; evaluates (agrees, partly agrees, qualifies) rather than just describes.
Level 3 (11-15 marks): clear and relevant evaluation of the statement; clear understanding of the writer's methods; a relevant range of quotations; clear comments on effects on the reader.
Level 2 and below (1-10 marks): some or simple evaluation; some reference to methods; quotations sometimes relevant; may retell the story.

Valid points include: flickering lights; baby crying; repetition in the businessman's actions; the interrupted announcement; 'mid-breath' (personification / human vulnerability); paradox 'so cold it burned'; vague 'something' and 'dark shape'; slow movement 'walking slowly' builds dread; final one-line paragraph and plain understatement. Strong answers evaluate which method is most effective and why.
questions.tip: Evaluate: say which method works BEST and why. That judgement is what separates level 4 from level 3.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 4

Source: the opening of a novel set in a village during a drought.

By August, the river had become a rumour.

The old people of Kesra still talked about it as if it were there, pointing down the valley to where it used to run, wide and brown and generous. But the children had never seen it. To them, the riverbed was simply a road of cracked clay, split into a thousand pale tiles that crunched underfoot like broken plates.

Every morning, before the heat rose, Nadia walked to the well with two plastic jerrycans. The path was three kilometres long. She knew every stone on it. She knew the thorn bush that snagged her sleeve, the dead acacia where the vultures waited, the place where the ground dipped and the air went suddenly cooler, as though remembering something.

The well was deeper every week. Or perhaps the water was shallower. It came to the same thing.

Today, when she lowered the bucket, she heard it knock against stone. Not splash. Knock.

She stood very still. The sun had cleared the hills now and was pressing on the back of her neck like a hot hand. Behind her, in the village, a goat bleated. Ahead of her, the dark mouth of the well said nothing at all.

Focus this part of your answer on the second half of the source, from 'Every morning, before the heat rose' to the end.

A student said, 'In this part of the story, the writer shows that Nadia is strong, but the landscape is stronger.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
- consider your own impressions of Nadia and the landscape
- evaluate how the writer creates these impressions
- support your response with references to the text.
questions.answer: I agree. Nadia's strength is shown through her routine: she walks three kilometres every morning with 'two plastic jerrycans', and the repetition of 'She knew' suggests mastery of a hard, dangerous path. However, the landscape seems to be winning. The 'dead acacia where the vultures waited' introduces death, and 'waited' suggests patience, as if the land expects to outlast her. The short paragraph 'The well was deeper every week. Or perhaps the water was shallower. It came to the same thing.' is flat and resigned, showing that her effort cannot change the situation. The climax 'Not splash. Knock.' uses minor sentences to emphasise the horror of hitting stone. The sun is 'pressing on the back of her neck like a hot hand', a personification that makes nature physically dominant, and the well's 'dark mouth' 'said nothing at all'. Nadia stands 'very still', which suggests her strength has met its limit.
ms: Level 4 (16-20 marks): critical, detailed and convincing evaluation of the statement; shows perceptive understanding of the writer's methods and how they create effects; a judicious range of quotations; evaluates (agrees, partly agrees, qualifies) rather than just describes.
Level 3 (11-15 marks): clear and relevant evaluation of the statement; clear understanding of the writer's methods; a relevant range of quotations; clear comments on effects on the reader.
Level 2 and below (1-10 marks): some or simple evaluation; some reference to methods; quotations sometimes relevant; may retell the story.

Valid points include: routine and endurance; 'She knew every stone' (repetition); vultures waiting; resigned tone of 'It came to the same thing'; contrast 'Not splash. Knock.'; personification of the sun ('hot hand') and the well ('dark mouth... said nothing'); her stillness at the end. Higher answers may argue the landscape is not 'stronger' but simply indifferent.
questions.tip: Q4 is worth 20 marks: spend 20 minutes. Take a clear stance on the statement, use 'the writer' throughout, and judge HOW WELL the methods work, not just what they are.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 4

Source: the opening of a novel set on a London housing estate.

The roof of Hartley Tower was the only place where Kieran could hear himself think.

Twenty-two floors below, the estate went about its evening business. Car alarms. A dog that never stopped barking. Somebody's music thumping out of an open window, the bass so heavy it seemed to come up through the concrete and into his trainers. From up here it all sounded small, like a radio left on in another room.

He sat with his back against the water tank, knees pulled up, and watched the city switch itself on. One by one the windows lit: yellow, white, the cold blue flicker of televisions. Further out, the towers of the City glittered like a mouthful of gold teeth.

His mum thought he was at Dev's. Dev thought he was at home. Nobody knew about the roof, and that was the point.

He took the letter out of his pocket. He had read it so many times that he could have recited it, but he unfolded it anyway, smoothing it flat against his knee. The paper was thin. The words were not.

We are pleased to offer you a place.

He looked out at the lights, and for the first time in his life, they looked like they were waiting for him.

Focus this part of your answer on the second half of the source, from 'His mum thought he was at Dev's.' to the end.

A student said, 'The writer makes the reader feel proud of Kieran by the end of this part of the story.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
- consider your own impressions of Kieran
- evaluate how the writer creates these impressions
- support your response with references to the text.
questions.answer: I mostly agree. The writer first creates sympathy: the balanced sentences 'His mum thought he was at Dev's. Dev thought he was at home.' show he has nobody to share his feelings with, and 'that was the point' suggests he guards his hopes carefully. His care with the letter, 'smoothing it flat against his knee', shows how much it matters. The contrast 'The paper was thin. The words were not.' turns an ordinary object into something weighty, building anticipation. The italic-style one-line paragraph 'We are pleased to offer you a place.' is the moment of pride, delivered simply so the reader feels the impact. The final sentence, 'for the first time in his life, they looked like they were waiting for him', makes the reader proud because it suggests a lifetime of feeling shut out has ended. However, the secrecy also suggests he cannot yet share his success, so pride is mixed with a sense of loneliness.
ms: Level 4 (16-20 marks): critical, detailed and convincing evaluation of the statement; shows perceptive understanding of the writer's methods and how they create effects; a judicious range of quotations; evaluates (agrees, partly agrees, qualifies) rather than just describes.
Level 3 (11-15 marks): clear and relevant evaluation of the statement; clear understanding of the writer's methods; a relevant range of quotations; clear comments on effects on the reader.
Level 2 and below (1-10 marks): some or simple evaluation; some reference to methods; quotations sometimes relevant; may retell the story.

Valid points include: secrecy shown in balanced sentences; 'that was the point'; repeated reading of the letter shows importance; contrast 'thin' / 'not'; withheld then revealed news; 'for the first time in his life' implies past exclusion; lights 'waiting for him' suggests future success. Strong answers may qualify: pride is mixed with sadness that nobody knows.
questions.tip: Q4 is worth 20 marks: spend 20 minutes. Take a clear stance on the statement, use 'the writer' throughout, and judge HOW WELL the methods work, not just what they are.

questions.q: A Q4 statement says: 'The writer makes the old shopkeeper seem lonely.' Which opening sentence would best set up a Level 4 response?
options: I agree because he is lonely.
In this essay I am going to write about loneliness.
The writer uses lots of techniques such as similes and metaphors.
I largely agree: the writer presents Mr Abernethy as isolated by a town that has moved on without him, though the girl's arrival suggests his loneliness may be about to end.
ms: C takes a clear, nuanced stance, links to the writer's methods and signals a developed argument. The others are vague or do not evaluate.
questions.tip: Start Q4 with a thesis: how far you agree and why, in one sentence.

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

Your local council is creating a booklet of creative writing about the area.

Write a description of a street market at dawn as suggested by this picture.

(The picture shows: a narrow market street just before sunrise. Stallholders are unloading crates of fruit from a van. Strings of bare bulbs hang between the stalls. Steam rises from a tea urn. The sky is pale pink above dark rooftops, and the ground is wet.)

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Plan (drop, shift, zoom, flash, echo):
1. Drop: the market before it wakes, darkness and silence, one bulb flickering on.
2. Shift: the stallholders arrive, sound and movement, unloading crates.
3. Zoom: a single detail, an old woman's hands arranging pomegranates.
4. Flash: brief memory or contrast, how the street looks at midday.
5. Echo: return to the bulbs as they are switched off at sunrise.

Opening paragraph:
At five o'clock, the market is still holding its breath. The stalls stand skeletal in the dark, their canvas roofs sagging with last night's rain, and the cobbles gleam like the backs of sleeping fish. Then, with a faint electric cough, the first bulb flickers awake. Another follows. Another. Soon a string of tiny suns sways between the stalls, and beneath them the street begins, slowly, reluctantly, to remember what it is for.

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of people of your own age.

Write a story about a character who discovers something they were never supposed to find.

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Plan:
1. Open in a quiet, ordinary moment: Leah clearing her late grandfather's shed.
2. The find: a biscuit tin hidden under the floorboards, heavier than it should be.
3. Build: inside, letters addressed to a woman Leah has never heard of, all returned unopened.
4. Turning point: the last letter is addressed to Leah herself, dated the year she was born.
5. Ending: she does not open it yet. End on her hand on the envelope, the light fading.

Opening paragraph:
The shed smelled of creosote and old rain, and of something else I couldn't name, something like the inside of a library. Grandad had kept it locked for as long as I could remember. 'Mice,' he used to say, tapping the side of his nose. 'And secrets.' I had always assumed he was joking about the secrets. Now, three weeks after the funeral, I knelt on the splintered floor with a crowbar in my hand and realised he had never been joking about anything.

The Ferris wheel has not turned in eleven years. Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

Your school is producing an anthology of short stories.

Write the opening part of a story that begins with the sentence: 'The door had been locked for twenty years.'

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Plan:
1. The door: description and history in a few lines only.
2. Character: Mrs Okafor, the caretaker, the only one with a key, retiring tomorrow.
3. Tension: she has promised never to open it. Tonight she decides to.
4. The moment: the key turns; the smell of dust and lavender.
5. Ending: a light is already on inside.

Opening paragraph:
The door had been locked for twenty years. It stood at the end of the east corridor, painted the same institutional green as the walls, so that most pupils walked past it without a second glance, the way you ignore a word you have read a thousand times. Only Mrs Okafor ever looked at it. Every evening, as she pushed her trolley of mops towards the exit, she paused, just for a second, and rested her palm flat against the wood, as if checking for a heartbeat.

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

You are entering a creative writing competition run by a national newspaper.

Write a story about a journey that does not go to plan.

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.

Plan:
1. In medias res: the car has stopped on a mountain road; snow is falling.
2. Characters: Sam and his older brother Theo, not speaking after an argument.
3. Problem: no phone signal, darkness coming.

The engine died with a cough, a shudder and then a silence so complete I could hear the snow settling on the roof. Theo turned the key again. Nothing. He turned it again, harder, as if the car might respond to anger. 'Don't,' I said, but he did it a third time, and the dashboard lights flickered once, apologetically, and went out. Outside, the mountain road vanished into white. We had not spoken in two hours. It looked as though we were going to have plenty of time to start.

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

A creative writing anthology for teenagers is looking for stories about change.

Write a story about a moment when everything changed.

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Plan:
1. Before: an ordinary Friday at the barber's, banter, the radio on.
2. The moment: the phone call (keep the detail of what happened off-page).
3. Slow motion: the clippers still buzzing, the hair falling, noticing tiny things.
4. After: walking home; the street looks the same but feels different.
5. Ending: return to the barber's mirror image (cyclical), seeing himself differently.

Opening paragraph:
It was the kind of Friday that doesn't ask to be remembered. The barber's on West Green Road was loud with radio and gossip, and Uncle Kofi was arguing with a customer about football while the clippers buzzed against the back of my neck like a lazy bee. I remember the smell of the aftershave. I remember that the clock above the mirror was eight minutes fast, because it always was. I remember all of it, every pointless detail, because forty seconds later my phone rang, and nothing afterwards was ever quite the same shape.

Technical accuracy, Level 4 (13-16 marks): sentence demarcation consistently secure and accurate; a wide range of punctuation used with a high level of accuracy; a full range of sentence forms used for effect; Standard English used consistently with secure control of complex grammar; high accuracy in spelling, including ambitious vocabulary.

Technical accuracy, Level 3 (9-12 marks): sentence demarcation mostly secure; a range of punctuation, mostly accurate; a variety of sentence forms for effect; mostly Standard English with controlled grammar; generally accurate spelling, including complex and irregular words.

Grade 8 benchmark: a deliberately shaped piece (not a list of senses or a full life story), where every paragraph has a job, sentence lengths change for effect, and there are almost no technical errors.

Strong features in this response: retrospective first-person narration; foreshadowing in the first sentence; anaphora ('I remember...') to slow time; vivid, specific setting; simile ('like a lazy bee'); final sentence that withholds the event to build tension; a planned cyclical ending.
questions.tip: Withholding is a powerful structural tool: you do not have to show the dramatic event directly. Focus on the moments around it.

questions.q: Paper 1 Question 5: which plan is most likely to produce a Level 4 descriptive piece about a train station?
options: Write as many similes and metaphors as possible in every sentence
Describe what you see, then hear, then smell, then taste, then touch
Tell the full story of a character's journey from waking up to arriving home
Begin with a wide view of the empty station at night, narrow to one detail, shift time to the morning rush, and end by echoing the opening image
ms: C has a crafted structure with deliberate shifts in focus and time and a cyclical ending. A is formulaic, B turns description into narrative, D overloads devices without control.
questions.tip: Structure is part of the 24 content and organisation marks. A five-senses list is predictable and rarely reaches Level 4.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1

Source A: an article from a national newspaper website, written in the 2020s by a parent in London.

Every weekday at 8.15, I walk my daughter to school along one of the busiest roads in north London. It takes eleven minutes. In that time, according to the little monitor clipped to her rucksack, she breathes some of the dirtiest air in the country. She is six.

I bought the monitor out of curiosity. I kept it out of fury. Each evening I download the data and watch the line spike, red and jagged, every time a lorry idles at the lights. The worst readings come not from the main road but from the school gate itself, where engines run while parents chat.

Read again the first two paragraphs of Source A.

Choose four statements below which are TRUE.
A. The writer walks her daughter to school every weekday.
B. The walk to school takes fifteen minutes.
C. The monitor is clipped to her daughter's rucksack.
D. The writer's daughter is nine years old.
E. The writer bought the monitor out of curiosity.
F. The writer downloads the data every morning.
G. The readings spike when lorries idle at the lights.
H. The worst readings come from the main road.
questions.answer: A, C, E, G
ms: 1 mark: A (every weekday at 8.15)
1 mark: C (clipped to her rucksack)
1 mark: E (bought it out of curiosity)
1 mark: G (spikes when a lorry idles)

Award 1 mark for each correct statement identified, up to 4. The question says choose a maximum of four: do not choose more than four. Statements must be judged on the named lines only. B is false (eleven minutes); D is false (she is six); F is false (each evening); H is false (the worst readings come from the school gate).
questions.tip: Read the statements word by word: distractors usually change one detail (a number, 'all' instead of 'some', a feeling the writer never states).

Paper 2 Question 1

Source B: a letter written in 1880 by a young man living in London to his sister in the countryside.

It came down on Tuesday afternoon like a great yellow blanket, and it has not lifted since. The gas lamps are lit at noon, yet they give no more light than a dying candle. Carriages creep along the Strand with boys running before them bearing torches, and even so I heard two collide with a most dreadful crash outside the bank.

The air itself has a taste, Harriet: sulphurous and bitter, like the inside of a kettle. It blackens the collar of every shirt within an hour. Poor Mrs Dalby, our landlady, coughs all night long, and the doctor says half the parish is in the same condition.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source B?
options: The gas lamps were lit at noon
The fog came down on a Monday morning
Two carriages collided outside a church
The landlady's cough was cured by the doctor
ms: The text says 'The gas lamps are lit at noon'. The fog came on Tuesday afternoon, the collision was outside the bank, and the doctor cured nobody.
questions.tip: Read the statements word by word: distractors usually change one detail (a number, 'all' instead of 'some', a feeling the writer never states).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1

Source A: a post from a family travel blog, written in the 2020s.

I'll be honest: I booked the trip expecting to hate it. Three days in a British seaside town in October, with two teenagers and a dog, sounded less like a holiday and more like a punishment.

I was wrong. Gloriously, embarrassingly wrong.

Yes, it rained. It rained sideways, upwards, and at one point, I swear, in a full circle. But there is something about a grey English beach that makes you feel more alive than any sunlounger ever could. We walked for miles along the tideline, collecting sea glass the colour of boiled sweets. We ate chips out of paper with our fingers turning blue. My son, who has not voluntarily left his bedroom in two years, challenged me to a race along the pier and actually laughed when he lost.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The writer's son won the race along the pier
The writer expected to enjoy the trip
The writer went on the trip in August
ms: 'We walked for miles along the tideline, collecting sea glass'. The trip was in October, she expected to hate it, and her son lost the race.
questions.tip: Read the statements word by word: distractors usually change one detail (a number, 'all' instead of 'some', a feeling the writer never states).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1

Source B: an extract from a letter to a magazine, written in 1863 by a gentleman describing a day trip to the coast.

It was my misfortune last Monday to travel to the coast by one of those cheap excursion trains which the railway companies now offer to the labouring classes. I had been assured that the sea air would restore my nerves. It did nothing of the kind.

The carriage, built to hold eight, contained fourteen persons, three baskets of provisions and an infant of remarkable lung power. Upon arrival, the whole multitude poured onto the sands like water from a burst dam. They shrieked; they paddled; they consumed whelks by the pint. A brass band played without mercy from ten o'clock until dusk.

Which statement is FALSE according to this part of Source B?
options: The carriage was built to hold fourteen people
A brass band played until dusk
He had been told the sea air would restore his nerves
The writer travelled on a cheap excursion train
ms: The carriage was built to hold eight but contained fourteen persons. The other three statements are true.
questions.tip: Questions asking for the FALSE statement are easy to misread. Underline the word FALSE before you start.

Source A: an opinion column from a newspaper, written in the 2020s.

When I was nine, my summer holidays had one rule: be home when the streetlights come on. Between breakfast and dusk, my friends and I roamed. We built dens in the scrubland behind the garages. The writer and friends built dens behind the garages
The writer had to be home by six o'clock as a child

Paper 2 Question 1

Source A: an extract from a letter written in 1831 by a young woman describing her first journey by train.

Yesterday I travelled upon the railway for the first time, and I scarcely know how to set down what I felt. My uncle had warned me that the human body was not made to move at such a pace, and that I might find my breath sucked clean out of me. I am pleased to report that I am still breathing, though I confess I held my breath for the better part of the first mile.

Then the speed increased, and increased again, until the hedgerows ran together into a green smear and the cattle in the fields seemed to be flung backwards by an invisible hand.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The engine was silent at the platform
The writer's uncle was excited about the railway
Her bonnet flew out of the window
The writer held her breath for most of the first mile
ms: 'I confess I held my breath for the better part of the first mile.' The uncle warned her, the bonnet landed in a stranger's lap, and the engine was hissing.

Paper 2 Question 1

Source B: an extract from a magazine feature, written in the 2020s, about a ride in a driverless taxi.

The car arrived with nobody in it. That was the first shock. It pulled up at the kerb, indicated politely, and unlocked its own doors, like a butler who had decided he no longer needed a body.

I climbed into the back seat. The steering wheel turned by itself, smooth and unhurried, as we eased into the traffic. For the first five minutes I gripped the door handle so tightly my knuckles ached. For the next five I filmed everything on my phone. By the fifteenth minute, to my own surprise, I was bored.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source B?
options: The writer felt bored by the fifteenth minute
A safety driver sat in the front of the car
The car drove onto the pavement to pick the writer up
The writer filmed the journey for the first five minutes

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1

Source B: an extract from a letter to a magazine, written in 1863 by a gentleman describing a day trip to the coast.

I do not deny that these people enjoyed themselves. Indeed, I never saw faces so red with happiness. A clerk beside me declared it the finest day of his life, and I believe he meant it. But I confess I longed for the quiet resorts of my boyhood, when a gentleman might walk the promenade without being struck by a donkey.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source B?
options: The writer felt refreshed when he returned home
The writer plans to make the trip again next year
The writer denies that the crowd enjoyed themselves
A clerk said it was the finest day of his life
