questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an article from a national newspaper website, written in the 2020s by a parent in London.

Every weekday at 8.15, I walk my daughter to school along one of the busiest roads in north London. It takes eleven minutes. In that time, according to the little monitor clipped to her rucksack, she breathes some of the dirtiest air in the country. She is six.

I bought the monitor out of curiosity. I kept it out of fury. Each evening I download the data and watch the line spike, red and jagged, every time a lorry idles at the lights. The worst readings come not from the main road but from the school gate itself, where engines run while parents chat.

We like to think dirty air belongs to the past: to Dickens, to chimney sweeps, to fog so thick you could lose your own hand in it. It does not. Our pollution has simply become invisible. You cannot see it, smell it or taste it, which makes it far easier to ignore.

But my daughter's lungs are not ignoring it. Doctors now link poor air to asthma and to weaker lung growth in children. Clean air is not a luxury. It is the least we owe our children.

----------

Source B: a letter written in 1880 by a young man living in London to his sister in the countryside.

My dear Harriet,

You asked me to describe a London fog, and I confess I hardly know where to begin, for I have been living inside one these four days and can scarcely see the end of my own pen.

It came down on Tuesday afternoon like a great yellow blanket, and it has not lifted since. The gas lamps are lit at noon, yet they give no more light than a dying candle. Carriages creep along the Strand with boys running before them bearing torches, and even so I heard two collide with a most dreadful crash outside the bank.

The air itself has a taste, Harriet: sulphurous and bitter, like the inside of a kettle. It blackens the collar of every shirt within an hour. Poor Mrs Dalby, our landlady, coughs all night long, and the doctor says half the parish is in the same condition.

Yet the strangest thing is how calmly the people bear it. They grumble, to be sure, but they go about their business as if choking were simply the price of living in the greatest city in the world. I cannot decide whether this is courage or madness.

Your affectionate brother, Edward

The air pollution described in the two sources is different.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: In Source B the pollution is visible and overwhelming: the fog is 'a great yellow blanket' and Edward 'can scarcely see the end of my own pen', which suggests it dominates every part of daily life. In Source A, by contrast, the pollution has 'become invisible'; it can only be detected by 'the little monitor', implying that modern danger is hidden and easier to ignore. The effects also differ. In 1880 they are immediate and obvious: shirts are blackened 'within an hour' and the landlady 'coughs all night long'. The modern writer focuses on longer-term, unseen harm to children's 'lung growth', suggesting a slower, more sinister threat. Finally, the people of 1880 bear it 'calmly' as 'the price of living in the greatest city', whereas the modern writer responds with 'fury', implying that attitudes have shifted from acceptance to anger.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): some or simple differences; may paraphrase without inference; may only use one source.
Note: no credit for analysing language techniques here. This question rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.

Valid differences include: visible (B: 'yellow blanket') vs invisible (A: 'become invisible'); immediate physical effects (B: blackened collars, coughing) vs measured data and long-term health risks (A: monitor, 'asthma', 'lung growth'); acceptance (B: 'calmly... the price of living') vs anger and a call for change (A: 'fury', 'the least we owe'); source of pollution: coal smoke / fog (B, 'sulphurous') vs traffic and idling engines (A).
questions.tip: Q2 is about WHAT is different, not HOW it is written. Use comparative connectives, quote from both sources, and make an inference for each quotation.

Source A: a post from a family travel blog, written in the 2020s.

I was wrong. Gloriously, embarrassingly wrong.

My son, who has not voluntarily left his bedroom in two years, challenged me to a race along the pier and actually laughed when he lost.

No queue at passport control. No two-hour delay. No sunburn. Just salt, wind and the sort of conversation you can only have when nobody has any signal.

Next year, everyone wants to go back. I have already booked.

----------

Source B: an extract from a letter to a magazine, written in 1863 by a gentleman describing a day trip to the coast.

It was my misfortune last Monday to travel to the coast by one of those cheap excursion trains which the railway companies now offer to the labouring classes. I had been assured that the sea air would restore my nerves. It did nothing of the kind.

The carriage, built to hold eight, contained fourteen persons, three baskets of provisions and an infant of remarkable lung power. Upon arrival, the whole multitude poured onto the sands like water from a burst dam. They shrieked; they paddled; they consumed whelks by the pint. A brass band played without mercy from ten o'clock until dusk.

I do not deny that these people enjoyed themselves. Indeed, I never saw faces so red with happiness. A clerk beside me declared it the finest day of his life, and I believe he meant it. But I confess I longed for the quiet resorts of my boyhood, when a gentleman might walk the promenade without being struck by a donkey.

I returned home more exhausted than when I set out, and I shall not repeat the experiment.

The writers' experiences of the seaside are different.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: The modern writer's experience is joyful and surprising. She expected 'a punishment' but was 'gloriously, embarrassingly wrong', suggesting the trip exceeded her expectations. The 1863 writer's experience is the opposite: the sea air 'did nothing of the kind', implying disappointment. The settings differ: Source A describes an empty, peaceful beach where the family 'walked for miles', whereas Source B describes a crowded beach where a 'multitude poured onto the sands', suggesting chaos. In Source A, family connection is central, as her withdrawn son 'actually laughed', while the Victorian writer is isolated, longing for 'the quiet resorts of my boyhood'. Finally, she is coming back ('I have already booked'), but he 'shall not repeat the experiment', which shows their opposite conclusions.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): some or simple differences; may paraphrase without inference; may only use one source.
Note: no credit for analysing language techniques here. This question rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.

Valid differences include: enjoyment vs exhaustion; exceeded expectations vs failed expectations; quiet empty beach vs crowded noisy sands; family bonding vs social discomfort (class difference: 'labouring classes'); returning vs never repeating. Higher answers may infer that the Victorian writer's snobbery shapes his experience.
questions.tip: Q2 is about WHAT is different, not HOW it is written. Use comparative connectives, quote from both sources, and make an inference for each quotation.

Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an opinion column from a newspaper, written in the 2020s.

When I was nine, my summer holidays had one rule: be home when the streetlights come on. Between breakfast and dusk, my friends and I roamed. We built dens in the scrubland behind the garages. We fell out of trees and climbed straight back up them. Nobody knew exactly where we were, and nobody seemed to mind.

Today, my nine-year-old nephew is not allowed to walk to the end of his road alone. His days are timetabled from start to finish: tutoring, swimming, coding club, a play date arranged by text three weeks in advance. Some researchers claim that the area in which children are free to wander has shrunk dramatically in just a few generations.

I understand why. Roads are busier. The news is full of fear. But in protecting children from every scraped knee, we may be robbing them of something precious: the chance to get lost, to be bored, to solve their own problems.

Childhood is not a dress rehearsal for adult life. It is a life in itself, and children deserve to live it.

----------

Source B: an extract from a report written in 1842 by a visitor to a cotton mill in the north of England.

I visited the mill at seven o'clock in the morning, by which hour the children had already been at their labour for an hour and a half. The noise of the machinery was so tremendous that I could not hear my own voice, and the air was thick with a fine white fluff that settled upon the hair and eyelashes of every worker like a premature old age.

Among them I observed a little girl, not above eight years of age, whose task was to crawl beneath the moving frames and gather up the loose cotton. She did this with great quickness, for, as the overseer informed me, a slow child might lose a finger. I asked her how long she worked each day. 'Twelve hours, sir,' she replied, 'and longer when the orders are heavy.'

She had never been to school. She could not read her own name. When I asked what she did for amusement, she looked at me as if I had spoken in a foreign tongue.

I came away sick at heart. A nation that grinds its children into thread has no right to call itself civilised.

The childhoods described in the two sources are different.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: The writer of Source A remembers a childhood of freedom, where 'nobody knew exactly where we were', implying trust and independence. The child in Source B has no freedom at all: she has worked 'an hour and a half' before seven, so her day belongs entirely to the mill. Play is central to the first childhood, as children 'built dens' and climbed trees, but the mill girl does not even understand the idea of 'amusement', looking at the visitor 'as if I had spoken in a foreign tongue', which suggests that play has been completely erased from her life. The risks also differ. In Source A the dangers are minor, a 'scraped knee', whereas in Source B a slow child 'might lose a finger', implying serious, permanent harm. Interestingly, the modern nephew in Source A is also controlled, but by timetables and adult protection rather than by work, so both writers suggest that adults shape childhood, for very different reasons.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): some or simple differences; may paraphrase without inference; may only use one source.
Note: no credit for analysing language techniques here. This question rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.

Valid differences include: freedom and roaming vs labour and confinement; play vs no concept of amusement; minor risks vs serious injury; education (the nephew's tutoring) vs no schooling ('could not read her own name'); control by protective adults vs control by economic exploitation. Level 4 answers may make a perceptive link (both children's lives are controlled by adults).
questions.tip: A perceptive link between the sources (a hidden similarity inside the difference) can push a strong answer into Level 4.

Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an extract from a letter written in 1831 by a young woman describing her first journey by train.

Yesterday I travelled upon the railway for the first time, and I scarcely know how to set down what I felt. My uncle had warned me that the human body was not made to move at such a pace, and that I might find my breath sucked clean out of me. I am pleased to report that I am still breathing, though I confess I held my breath for the better part of the first mile.

The engine stood hissing at the platform like some great black beast impatient for its dinner. When at last it moved, it did so with a jolt that threw my bonnet into the lap of a stranger. Then the speed increased, and increased again, until the hedgerows ran together into a green smear and the cattle in the fields seemed to be flung backwards by an invisible hand.

Some passengers laughed. One lady fainted. For myself, I was torn between terror and delight, and could not tell which had the upper hand.

I am certain of one thing only: the world will not be the same again. Distance, which God set between towns, has been conquered by a kettle on wheels.

----------

Source B: an extract from a magazine feature, written in the 2020s, about a ride in a driverless taxi.

The car arrived with nobody in it. That was the first shock. It pulled up at the kerb, indicated politely, and unlocked its own doors, like a butler who had decided he no longer needed a body.

I climbed into the back seat. The steering wheel turned by itself, smooth and unhurried, as we eased into the traffic. For the first five minutes I gripped the door handle so tightly my knuckles ached. For the next five I filmed everything on my phone. By the fifteenth minute, to my own surprise, I was bored.

That, I think, is the strangest part. Something that would have seemed like witchcraft a decade ago became ordinary before I had even reached my destination. Humans adapt astonishingly fast.

And yet I stepped out with an uneasy feeling. Who decided how this car would behave in an emergency? Whose life would it choose to protect? The machine had not asked my opinion. It had simply driven, perfectly, and left me with questions it could not answer.

The two writers' experiences of new transport technology are different.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: Both writers are nervous at first, but in different ways. The 1831 writer's fear is physical: she was warned her breath might be 'sucked clean out' and she 'held my breath', suggesting she feared for her body. The modern writer's anxiety fades quickly: by the fifteenth minute 'I was bored', implying that technology becomes normal almost instantly. The earlier journey is dramatic and chaotic, with a 'jolt' that threw her bonnet and a lady who 'fainted', whereas the driverless car is calm and polite, easing 'smooth and unhurried' into traffic. Their final thoughts differ most. The Victorian writer is certain 'the world will not be the same again', focusing on the triumph of conquering distance, while the modern writer leaves with 'an uneasy feeling' and moral 'questions', suggesting a concern about who controls the technology.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): some or simple differences; may paraphrase without inference; may only use one source.
Note: no credit for analysing language techniques here. This question rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.

Valid differences include: physical fear vs quickly fading nervousness; chaos and drama (jolt, fainting) vs calm smoothness; human passengers' reactions (laughing, fainting) vs the writer alone; triumphant certainty vs moral unease; focus on speed and distance vs focus on control and ethics.
questions.tip: Q2 is about WHAT is different, not HOW it is written. Use comparative connectives, quote from both sources, and make an inference for each quotation.

Source B: a letter written in 1880 by a young man living in London to his sister in the countryside.

My dear Harriet,

You asked me to describe a London fog, and I confess I hardly know where to begin, for I have been living inside one these four days and can scarcely see the end of my own pen.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: In Source B the people of London accept the fog. They 'grumble' but 'go about their business', which suggests they see it as a normal part of city life. The writer of Source A reacts with 'fury', whereas Edward is uncertain, unable to decide if the people's calm is 'courage or madness'.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: a post from a family travel blog, written in the 2020s.

I'll be honest: I booked the trip expecting to hate it. Three days in a British seaside town in October, with two teenagers and a dog, sounded less like a holiday and more like a punishment.

I was wrong. Gloriously, embarrassingly wrong.

Yes, it rained. It rained sideways, upwards, and at one point, I swear, in a full circle. But there is something about a grey English beach that makes you feel more alive than any sunlounger ever could. We walked for miles along the tideline, collecting sea glass the colour of boiled sweets. We ate chips out of paper with our fingers turning blue. My son, who has not voluntarily left his bedroom in two years, challenged me to a race along the pier and actually laughed when he lost.

No queue at passport control. No two-hour delay. No sunburn. Just salt, wind and the sort of conversation you can only have when nobody has any signal.

Next year, everyone wants to go back. I have already booked.

----------

Source B: an extract from a letter to a magazine, written in 1863 by a gentleman describing a day trip to the coast.

It was my misfortune last Monday to travel to the coast by one of those cheap excursion trains which the railway companies now offer to the labouring classes. I had been assured that the sea air would restore my nerves. It did nothing of the kind.

The carriage, built to hold eight, contained fourteen persons, three baskets of provisions and an infant of remarkable lung power. Upon arrival, the whole multitude poured onto the sands like water from a burst dam. They shrieked; they paddled; they consumed whelks by the pint. A brass band played without mercy from ten o'clock until dusk.

I do not deny that these people enjoyed themselves. Indeed, I never saw faces so red with happiness. A clerk beside me declared it the finest day of his life, and I believe he meant it. But I confess I longed for the quiet resorts of my boyhood, when a gentleman might walk the promenade without being struck by a donkey.

I returned home more exhausted than when I set out, and I shall not repeat the experiment.

The crowds and other people described in the two sources are different.

Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences.
questions.answer: Source A presents a seaside with almost no crowds at all: there is 'no queue' and 'nobody has any signal', which implies the empty space is what allows real connection between family members. Source B is defined by its crowd: fourteen people squeezed into a carriage built for eight, and a 'multitude' pouring onto the sands. The writer of Source B sees these people from a distance, as 'the labouring classes', suggesting he views them as a different, slightly lower kind of person. By contrast, the people in Source A are her own family, and she watches them closely and warmly, noticing that her son 'actually laughed'. Despite his disapproval, the Victorian writer admits they had 'faces so red with happiness', so both texts suggest that the seaside makes people happy, even if he cannot share that happiness.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; makes insightful inferences (reads between the lines) about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts; clear, sustained links between the two.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences about differences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 and below (1-4 marks): some or simple differences; may paraphrase without inference; may only use one source.
Note: no credit for analysing language techniques here. This question rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.

Valid differences include: emptiness vs overcrowding; family vs strangers; warmth and closeness vs snobbish distance ('labouring classes'); quiet vs noise ('shrieked', brass band); a perceptive link that both texts show others' happiness.
questions.tip: Q2 is about WHAT is different, not HOW it is written. Use comparative connectives, quote from both sources, and make an inference for each quotation.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 2: which sentence would be credited most highly in a summary of differences?
options: While the modern beach is so empty that the family 'walked for miles', the Victorian sands are overrun by a 'multitude', suggesting that the earlier writer's discomfort comes as much from the crowd as from the place itself.
Source B uses a simile, 'like water from a burst dam', which is very effective.
Source A is written in the 2020s and Source B is written in 1863.
Source A is about the seaside and Source B is also about the seaside.
ms: C makes a clear difference, uses evidence from both sources and adds an inference. A analyses language (no credit in Q2), B is a similarity, D is a basic contextual fact with no inference.

How does the writer use language to describe the London fog?

The contrast between gas lamps 'lit at noon' and 'no more light than a dying candle' turns day into night, and 'dying' introduces a sense of decay. Edward appeals to the senses: the fog has 'a taste', and the adjectives 'sulphurous and bitter' are harsh, while the simile 'like the inside of a kettle' is domestic and grimy, making the reader almost taste the air. The direct address 'Harriet' adds intimacy, as if he wants his sister to share his shock. His closing antithesis, 'courage or madness', shows his mixed admiration and disbelief.

Paper 2 Question 3

You now need to refer only to Source B.

Source B: an extract from a report written in 1842 by a visitor to a cotton mill in the north of England.

I visited the mill at seven o'clock in the morning, by which hour the children had already been at their labour for an hour and a half. The noise of the machinery was so tremendous that I could not hear my own voice, and the air was thick with a fine white fluff that settled upon the hair and eyelashes of every worker like a premature old age.

Among them I observed a little girl, not above eight years of age, whose task was to crawl beneath the moving frames and gather up the loose cotton. She did this with great quickness, for, as the overseer informed me, a slow child might lose a finger. I asked her how long she worked each day. 'Twelve hours, sir,' she replied, 'and longer when the orders are heavy.'

She had never been to school. She could not read her own name. When I asked what she did for amusement, she looked at me as if I had spoken in a foreign tongue.

I came away sick at heart. A nation that grinds its children into thread has no right to call itself civilised.

How does the writer use language to present the conditions in the mill?

[12 marks]
questions.answer: The writer uses language to shock the reader into moral outrage. The hyperbole 'so tremendous that I could not hear my own voice' suggests the noise drowns out humanity itself. The simile of fluff settling on the children 'like a premature old age' is especially powerful: it transforms a physical detail into a symbol of stolen childhood, as the white fluff resembles grey hair. The verb 'crawl' dehumanises the girl, making her seem animal-like, and the overseer's casual warning that 'a slow child might lose a finger' is reported in a flat, matter-of-fact way, which makes the cruelty more disturbing. Direct speech, 'Twelve hours, sir', gives the girl a voice and makes the abuse undeniable. Finally, the metaphor 'grinds its children into thread' presents the nation as a machine consuming its young, and the emotive 'sick at heart' shows the writer's personal distress.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight; judicious, precise quotations; sophisticated and accurate terminology; explores how word choices build the writer's tone and attitude.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clearly explains the effects of language; relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 and below (1-6 marks): simple or partial comments; references sometimes relevant; terminology may be inaccurate.

Valid points include: precise time 'seven o'clock... an hour and a half' shows long hours; hyperbole about noise; simile 'like a premature old age'; 'crawl' (dehumanising); flat reporting of 'might lose a finger'; direct speech; repetitive negatives 'She had never... She could not...'; simile 'as if I had spoken in a foreign tongue'; metaphor 'grinds its children into thread'; emotive 'sick at heart'; moral judgement 'no right to call itself civilised'.
questions.tip: At Level 4, link language to purpose: this writer wants to provoke reform, so every image works to shock.

Paper 2 Question 3

You now need to refer only to Source A.

Source A: an article from a national newspaper website, written in the 2020s by a parent in London.

Every weekday at 8.15, I walk my daughter to school along one of the busiest roads in north London. It takes eleven minutes. In that time, according to the little monitor clipped to her rucksack, she breathes some of the dirtiest air in the country. She is six.

I bought the monitor out of curiosity. I kept it out of fury. Each evening I download the data and watch the line spike, red and jagged, every time a lorry idles at the lights. The worst readings come not from the main road but from the school gate itself, where engines run while parents chat.

We like to think dirty air belongs to the past: to Dickens, to chimney sweeps, to fog so thick you could lose your own hand in it. It does not. Our pollution has simply become invisible. You cannot see it, smell it or taste it, which makes it far easier to ignore.

But my daughter's lungs are not ignoring it. Doctors now link poor air to asthma and to weaker lung growth in children. Clean air is not a luxury. It is the least we owe our children.

How does the writer use language to persuade the reader that air pollution is a serious problem?

[12 marks]
questions.answer: The writer opens with precise, personal detail, '8.15', 'eleven minutes', building credibility before the shocking short sentence 'She is six.', which creates an emotional punch. The antithesis 'I bought the monitor out of curiosity. I kept it out of fury.' shows a shift from interest to anger. The visual description of the data 'red and jagged' suggests danger and violence. She uses a list of Victorian clichés, 'Dickens... chimney sweeps... fog', to dismiss the idea that pollution is old-fashioned, followed by the blunt 'It does not.' The tricolon 'see it, smell it or taste it' emphasises invisibility. Personification, 'my daughter's lungs are not ignoring it', makes the body seem to fight back. The final short declaratives, 'Clean air is not a luxury. It is the least we owe our children', end on a moral imperative with the inclusive 'we'.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): analyses the effects of language in depth and with insight; judicious, precise quotations; sophisticated and accurate terminology; explores how word choices build the writer's tone and attitude.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clearly explains the effects of language; relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 and below (1-6 marks): simple or partial comments; references sometimes relevant; terminology may be inaccurate.

Valid points include: personal anecdote and precise numbers; short sentence 'She is six.'; antithesis curiosity / fury; 'red and jagged'; superlative 'some of the dirtiest air'; list of historical references; blunt 'It does not.'; tricolon 'see it, smell it or taste it'; personification of lungs; appeal to authority 'Doctors now link'; inclusive 'we' and 'our'; moral conclusion.

Paper 2 Question 3

You now need to refer only to Source B.

Source B: an extract from a magazine feature, written in the 2020s, about a ride in a driverless taxi.

The car arrived with nobody in it. That was the first shock. It pulled up at the kerb, indicated politely, and unlocked its own doors, like a butler who had decided he no longer needed a body.

I climbed into the back seat. The steering wheel turned by itself, smooth and unhurried, as we eased into the traffic. For the first five minutes I gripped the door handle so tightly my knuckles ached. For the next five I filmed everything on my phone. By the fifteenth minute, to my own surprise, I was bored.

That, I think, is the strangest part. Something that would have seemed like witchcraft a decade ago became ordinary before I had even reached my destination. Humans adapt astonishingly fast.

And yet I stepped out with an uneasy feeling. Who decided how this car would behave in an emergency? Whose life would it choose to protect? The machine had not asked my opinion. It had simply driven, perfectly, and left me with questions it could not answer.

How does the writer use language to describe the experience of riding in a driverless car?

[12 marks]
questions.answer: The writer uses short sentences and humour to convey surprise. 'The car arrived with nobody in it. That was the first shock.' is blunt and immediate. The simile 'like a butler who had decided he no longer needed a body' is comic but eerie, personifying the car as a polite servant while hinting at something unnatural. The steering wheel 'turned by itself', a phrase suggesting the supernatural. The time structure 'For the first five minutes... For the next five... By the fifteenth minute' tracks his emotions from fear ('knuckles ached') to excitement to boredom, showing how quickly the extraordinary becomes ordinary. 'Witchcraft' reinforces the sense of magic. Finally, rhetorical questions, 'Whose life would it choose to protect?', change the tone to moral unease, and the personification 'had not asked my opinion' suggests a loss of human control.

But I confess I longed for the quiet resorts of my boyhood, when a gentleman might walk the promenade without being struck by a donkey.

I returned home more exhausted than when I set out, and I shall not repeat the experiment.

Compare how the writers convey their different attitudes to the seaside.

- compare the methods the writers use to convey their attitudes to the seaside

[16 marks]
questions.answer: The modern writer celebrates the seaside, while the Victorian writer resents it, although both acknowledge that it makes others happy. The blogger uses an informal, self-mocking voice, 'I'll be honest', 'I swear', to build trust, so her conversion feels genuine. The Victorian writer uses formal, elaborate language, 'It was my misfortune', which creates an ironic, superior tone. Both use humour, but differently: her comic hyperbole about rain shows she can laugh at discomfort, whereas his bathos, 'struck by a donkey', mocks the crowd. Her view is shaped by family: the image of her son who 'actually laughed' is the emotional centre. His view is shaped by class; 'labouring classes' shows he sees the trip as something beneath him. They end in opposite places: she has 'already booked', he 'shall not repeat the experiment'. These attitudes reflect context: cheap railway excursions in the mid-1800s brought large working-class crowds to the seaside, whereas in the 2020s a quiet British beach is a welcome escape from crowded airports.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 4

Source A: an opinion column from a newspaper, written in the 2020s.

When I was nine, my summer holidays had one rule: be home when the streetlights come on. Between breakfast and dusk, my friends and I roamed. We built dens in the scrubland behind the garages. We fell out of trees and climbed straight back up them. Nobody knew exactly where we were, and nobody seemed to mind.

Today, my nine-year-old nephew is not allowed to walk to the end of his road alone. His days are timetabled from start to finish: tutoring, swimming, coding club, a play date arranged by text three weeks in advance. Some researchers claim that the area in which children are free to wander has shrunk dramatically in just a few generations.

I understand why. Roads are busier. The news is full of fear. But in protecting children from every scraped knee, we may be robbing them of something precious: the chance to get lost, to be bored, to solve their own problems.

Childhood is not a dress rehearsal for adult life. It is a life in itself, and children deserve to live it.

----------

Source B: an extract from a report written in 1842 by a visitor to a cotton mill in the north of England.

I visited the mill at seven o'clock in the morning, by which hour the children had already been at their labour for an hour and a half. The noise of the machinery was so tremendous that I could not hear my own voice, and the air was thick with a fine white fluff that settled upon the hair and eyelashes of every worker like a premature old age.

Among them I observed a little girl, not above eight years of age, whose task was to crawl beneath the moving frames and gather up the loose cotton. She did this with great quickness, for, as the overseer informed me, a slow child might lose a finger. I asked her how long she worked each day. 'Twelve hours, sir,' she replied, 'and longer when the orders are heavy.'

She had never been to school. She could not read her own name. When I asked what she did for amusement, she looked at me as if I had spoken in a foreign tongue.

I came away sick at heart. A nation that grinds its children into thread has no right to call itself civilised.

For this question, you need to refer to the whole of Source A, together with the whole of Source B.

Compare how the writers convey their different perspectives on childhood.

In your answer, you could:
- compare their different perspectives on childhood
- compare the methods the writers use to convey their perspectives on childhood
- support your response with references to both texts.

[16 marks]
questions.answer: Both writers believe children deserve a proper childhood, but the modern writer is nostalgic and gently critical, while the 1842 writer is horrified and condemning. Source A uses a personal anecdote of freedom, 'be home when the streetlights come on', and a warm, nostalgic tone. Source B uses eyewitness reporting and precise detail, 'seven o'clock', 'twelve hours', to build an authoritative case. The modern writer is balanced: 'I understand why' concedes that parents have reasons, before arguing that protection may be 'robbing' children. The Victorian writer allows no balance; the girl's direct speech and the simile 'like a premature old age' make exploitation undeniable. Both end with a moral statement: Source A's 'Childhood is not a dress rehearsal' and Source B's 'no right to call itself civilised'. However, the stakes differ enormously. The modern writer worries about lost boredom and adventure; the Victorian writer witnesses lost fingers and lost education. Their perspectives reflect their eras: industrial child labour in the 1840s versus modern anxiety about safety.

Level 3 (9-12 marks): clear and relevant comparison of perspectives; explains how writers' methods convey those perspectives; relevant quotations from both sources.
Level 2 and below (1-8 marks): some or simple comparison; may treat sources separately; methods identified rather than explained.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 4

Source A: an extract from a letter written in 1831 by a young woman describing her first journey by train.

Yesterday I travelled upon the railway for the first time, and I scarcely know how to set down what I felt. My uncle had warned me that the human body was not made to move at such a pace, and that I might find my breath sucked clean out of me. I am pleased to report that I am still breathing, though I confess I held my breath for the better part of the first mile.

The engine stood hissing at the platform like some great black beast impatient for its dinner. When at last it moved, it did so with a jolt that threw my bonnet into the lap of a stranger. Then the speed increased, and increased again, until the hedgerows ran together into a green smear and the cattle in the fields seemed to be flung backwards by an invisible hand.

Some passengers laughed. One lady fainted. For myself, I was torn between terror and delight, and could not tell which had the upper hand.

I am certain of one thing only: the world will not be the same again. Distance, which God set between towns, has been conquered by a kettle on wheels.

----------

Source B: an extract from a magazine feature, written in the 2020s, about a ride in a driverless taxi.

The car arrived with nobody in it. That was the first shock. It pulled up at the kerb, indicated politely, and unlocked its own doors, like a butler who had decided he no longer needed a body.

I climbed into the back seat. The steering wheel turned by itself, smooth and unhurried, as we eased into the traffic. For the first five minutes I gripped the door handle so tightly my knuckles ached. For the next five I filmed everything on my phone. By the fifteenth minute, to my own surprise, I was bored.

That, I think, is the strangest part. Something that would have seemed like witchcraft a decade ago became ordinary before I had even reached my destination. Humans adapt astonishingly fast.

And yet I stepped out with an uneasy feeling. Who decided how this car would behave in an emergency? Whose life would it choose to protect? The machine had not asked my opinion. It had simply driven, perfectly, and left me with questions it could not answer.

For this question, you need to refer to the whole of Source A, together with the whole of Source B.

Compare how the writers convey their different feelings about new transport technology.

In your answer, you could:
- compare their different feelings about new transport technology
- compare the methods the writers use to convey their feelings about new transport technology
- support your response with references to both texts.

[16 marks]
questions.answer: Both writers experience a mix of fear and wonder, but the 1831 writer ends in triumphant certainty while the modern writer ends in unease. The Victorian letter is lively and dramatic, using the metaphor of the engine as 'some great black beast impatient for its dinner' to make the technology seem alive and powerful. The modern writer also personifies the car, but as 'a butler', polite and controlled rather than wild. Both track a change in feeling. She is 'torn between terror and delight'; he moves from gripping the handle to being 'bored'. Their conclusions reveal different perspectives. She celebrates human achievement: 'Distance... has been conquered by a kettle on wheels', a comic yet awed metaphor. He raises rhetorical questions, 'Whose life would it choose to protect?', suggesting that modern technology brings moral problems as well as convenience. The difference reflects context: in 1831 the railway seemed to expand human power, while today automation raises fears about losing control.

Level 2 and below (1-8 marks): some or simple comparison; may treat sources separately; methods identified rather than explained.

Valid comparisons include: wonder and triumph vs boredom and unease; animal imagery (beast) vs servant imagery (butler); physical drama vs calm smoothness; both track changing emotions; triumphant final statement vs rhetorical questions; context of early industrial optimism vs modern concerns about AI and automation.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 4

Source A: an article from a national newspaper website, written in the 2020s by a parent in London.

Every weekday at 8.15, I walk my daughter to school along one of the busiest roads in north London. It takes eleven minutes. In that time, according to the little monitor clipped to her rucksack, she breathes some of the dirtiest air in the country. She is six.

I bought the monitor out of curiosity. I kept it out of fury. Each evening I download the data and watch the line spike, red and jagged, every time a lorry idles at the lights. The worst readings come not from the main road but from the school gate itself, where engines run while parents chat.

We like to think dirty air belongs to the past: to Dickens, to chimney sweeps, to fog so thick you could lose your own hand in it. It does not. Our pollution has simply become invisible. You cannot see it, smell it or taste it, which makes it far easier to ignore.

But my daughter's lungs are not ignoring it. Doctors now link poor air to asthma and to weaker lung growth in children. Clean air is not a luxury. It is the least we owe our children.

----------

Source B: a letter written in 1880 by a young man living in London to his sister in the countryside.

My dear Harriet,

You asked me to describe a London fog, and I confess I hardly know where to begin, for I have been living inside one these four days and can scarcely see the end of my own pen.

It came down on Tuesday afternoon like a great yellow blanket, and it has not lifted since. The gas lamps are lit at noon, yet they give no more light than a dying candle. Carriages creep along the Strand with boys running before them bearing torches, and even so I heard two collide with a most dreadful crash outside the bank.

The air itself has a taste, Harriet: sulphurous and bitter, like the inside of a kettle. It blackens the collar of every shirt within an hour. Poor Mrs Dalby, our landlady, coughs all night long, and the doctor says half the parish is in the same condition.

Yet the strangest thing is how calmly the people bear it. They grumble, to be sure, but they go about their business as if choking were simply the price of living in the greatest city in the world. I cannot decide whether this is courage or madness.

Your affectionate brother, Edward

For this question, you need to refer to the whole of Source A, together with the whole of Source B.

Compare how the writers convey their different attitudes towards the people around them.

[16 marks]
questions.answer: Edward observes the people around him with curiosity and a degree of admiration, whereas the modern writer views those around her with frustration. Edward describes Londoners who 'grumble, to be sure, but they go about their business', and his phrase 'the greatest city in the world' captures their pride. His closing antithesis, 'courage or madness', shows he is fascinated but undecided. He is also sympathetic towards 'Poor Mrs Dalby', the adjective 'poor' revealing compassion. The modern writer's attitude to others is critical: she highlights 'the school gate itself, where engines run while parents chat', an implicit accusation that adults are endangering children through carelessness. She uses the collective 'we' to share responsibility, 'the least we owe our children', which is persuasive but also includes herself. Edward's purpose is to inform and entertain his sister, so he reports others' behaviour; hers is to change behaviour, so she judges it.
ms: Level 4 (13-16 marks): compares ideas and perspectives in a perceptive, detailed way; analyses how each writer's methods convey their perspective; judicious quotations from both sources; shows insight into why the perspectives differ (purpose, audience, time period).
Level 3 (9-12 marks): clear and relevant comparison of perspectives; explains how writers' methods convey those perspectives; relevant quotations from both sources.
Level 2 and below (1-8 marks): some or simple comparison; may treat sources separately; methods identified rather than explained.

Valid comparisons include: curiosity vs frustration; sympathy for Mrs Dalby vs criticism of parents; 'courage or madness' (open) vs implicit accusation; inclusive 'we'; purpose of a private letter vs persuasive article; both show people accepting pollution, but the writers respond differently.
questions.tip: Compare throughout. Each paragraph should cover both sources: the writers' views, the methods that show those views, and why they differ.

'Cars should be banned from the area around every school. Children's health matters more than drivers' convenience.'

Write an article for a local newspaper in which you argue for or against this statement.

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Plan:
Headline: 'The School Run Is Choking Our Children'
1. Hook: anecdote of Year 7s walking through exhaust fumes at 8.30.
2. Evidence: idling engines at the gate; asthma; children are closer to exhaust height.
3. Counter-argument: parents who work, disabled access. Rebut: exemptions and 'school streets' schemes.
4. Benefits: safer roads, exercise, independence.
5. Ending: return to the opening image; call to action for the council.

Opening paragraph:
At 8.25 every morning, the road outside my school becomes a car park. Engines rumble. Horns blare. And through the haze, hundreds of children, some as young as eleven, walk with their faces at exactly the height of a car's exhaust pipe. We would never let a stranger blow smoke in a child's face. So why do we allow it, five days a week, at the one place children are supposed to be safe?

'Social media does more harm than good to teenagers. It should be banned for anyone under sixteen.'
