What a Level 4 response does here: a clear shape with a cyclical ending; small human portraits rather than a crowd; a touch of humour (the pigeon) to vary tone; precise London details; onomatopoeia and personification that serve the mood; accurate, varied punctuation (colon for a list, semicolons, dashes).
questions.tip: Even at Level 1 standard, plan the shape before you write. A simple five-part shape with an echoing ending lifts a response quickly.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

A national newspaper is running a short story competition for students. The theme is 'The Truth'.

Write a story in which a character has to decide whether to tell the truth.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. Hook: dialogue first. 'Did you see who did it?' The head of year is waiting for an answer. Freeze the moment.
2. Slow time: the narrator's thoughts in the three seconds before answering; sensory detail of the office (the radiator ticking, the fish tank).
3. Brief backstory: the narrator's best friend did it, and the friend has been having a hard time at home (implied, not explained).
4. Climax: the narrator lies, and the writing shows the physical feel of the lie.
5. Twist or consequence: walking out, the narrator sees another student (who was wrongly blamed) sitting outside the office.
6. Ending: an unresolved final line that turns the question back on the reader.

Sample opening:
'Did you see who did it?'
Mr Okafor asked it gently, which was worse. If he had shouted, I could have shouted back, or cried, or stared at the carpet until he gave up. But he just waited, his hands folded on the desk, and behind him the fish tank bubbled, and the radiator ticked, and somewhere down the corridor a door banged shut like a full stop.

What a Level 4 response does here: time slowed around a single decision rather than a long plot; dialogue used sparingly and correctly punctuated; tension built through sensory detail and polysyndeton; implicit characterisation; a moral twist that complicates the decision; an open, thought-provoking ending.
questions.tip: About 45 minutes: 5-10 planning, 30-35 writing, 5 proofreading. The real paper gives a choice of two tasks; pick the one you can shape best, not the one you like the sound of.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

Your English department is creating a display of descriptive writing called 'Hidden Places'.

Write a description of an old attic as suggested by this picture.

(The picture shows: a dusty attic lit by a single small window. Sunlight falls in a beam full of floating dust. Cardboard boxes are stacked unevenly, one labelled 'XMAS'. An old rocking horse stands in the corner with a missing ear. A suitcase lies open, with letters spilling out.)

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. Light: the single beam from the window, dust 'turning slowly like a galaxy'. Begin with the window as the only way in.
2. Wide: shapes in the gloom, boxes stacked like a crooked city skyline.
3. Zoom: the rocking horse with the missing ear, frozen mid-gallop; who rode it?
4. Zoom further: the open suitcase, letters spilling out; describe the handwriting, the faded stamps, without reading them in full.
5. Shift in time: a brief imagined memory of the attic in a past Christmas (the 'XMAS' box).
6. Echo: the beam of light has moved across the floor, measuring time passing.

Sample opening:
One window. That is all the attic allows itself: a single square of glass, no bigger than a book, set into the slope of the roof. Through it the afternoon comes in sideways, a long blade of light, and in that light the dust is turning, slowly, endlessly, like a galaxy that nobody has bothered to name.

questions.q:
Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

A website is publishing stories written by teenagers about friendship.

Write the opening part of a story about two friends who fall out.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan (opening only: no need to resolve everything):
1. Start at the end of the friendship: an empty seat on the bus where Jaden usually sits.
2. Rewind to the argument, told through fragments of dialogue and what was not said.
3. Focus on one small object that mattered to both (a shared pair of earphones, one bud each).
4. Present day: the narrator sees Jaden laughing with someone else at the bus stop.
5. End the opening on a choice: the narrator has one earphone in, the other hanging loose.

Sample opening:

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

A creative writing magazine is collecting descriptions of extreme weather.

Write a description of a city during a heatwave as suggested by this picture.

(The picture shows: a city street in blazing summer heat. The air above the road shimmers. People shelter in the narrow shade of buildings. A child runs through water from an open fire hydrant. A dog lies flat under a parked car. Shop awnings are pulled down. The sky is white and cloudless.)

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. The sky: white, not blue, like a lid on a pan. Extended metaphor of the city as something being cooked.
2. The road: shimmer, melting tar, the smell of hot rubber.
3. People: pressed into strips of shade 'like pages pressed into a book'; movement slowed to almost nothing.
4. Contrast: the child in the hydrant spray, the only fast, joyful thing on the street; shift to sound and colour.
5. Small detail: the dog under the car, one ear twitching.
6. Ending: evening, the first breath of cooler air, the city 'exhaling'; echo the pan-lid image as the lid lifts.

Sample opening:
The sky has stopped being blue. Somewhere around noon it gave up the effort and turned white, a flat, blank, glaring lid pressed down over the city, and underneath it everything is slowly, quietly cooking. The tarmac sweats. The railings are too hot to touch. Even the pigeons have abandoned the square, leaving it to the heat and to the long, wavering ghost of air that rises off the road and makes the buses look like they are melting.

Paper 1 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

Your school's student magazine is looking for exciting short stories.

Write a story that begins with the sentence: 'The lights went out at exactly midnight.'

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

You are advised to plan your answer. Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. The given sentence, then immediate sensory reaction: silence, the fridge stops humming.
2. Setting and character: the narrator alone at home, parents on a night shift; phone at 4 per cent.
3. Rising tension: a sound downstairs, built through short sentences and questions.
4. Turning point: the narrator goes down, torchlight showing only fragments.
5. Twist: it is the narrator's grandmother, who has come round to check on them because the whole street lost power, holding candles.
6. Ending: candlelight, tea, the lights come back on but they leave them off. Shift from fear to warmth.

Sample opening:
The lights went out at exactly midnight.
I know it was exactly midnight because I was watching the clock on my phone, waiting for it to turn, the way you do when you are meant to be asleep. 23:59. Then 00:00. Then nothing at all. The fridge downstairs stopped humming. The street lamp outside my window blinked out like a closing eye, and the dark came into my room all at once, thick and total, as if somebody had poured it in.

Source A: an article from a newspaper website, written in the 2020s, about cold-water swimming in London.

The thermometer on the jetty says four degrees. I have learned not to look at it.

1 mark: C ('seven in the morning')

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an article from a newspaper website, written in the 2020s, about cold-water swimming in London.

The thermometer on the jetty says four degrees. I have learned not to look at it.

It is seven in the morning on Hampstead Heath, the sky the colour of wet newspaper, and there are already eleven of us queuing on the wooden boards in dressing gowns and woolly hats. Nobody talks much. One woman, who tells me she is seventy-three, is doing star jumps. A man in a Santa hat is quietly weeping, though he insists this is 'just the wind'.

I started cold-water swimming two winters ago, after a year in which I had stopped sleeping, stopped running and very nearly stopped leaving the house. A friend dragged me here. I lasted forty seconds and swore, loudly and inventively, for all of them. Then I climbed out, shaking and scarlet, and felt something I had not felt in months: awake.

The science is still catching up. Some researchers believe cold water may lift mood and reduce inflammation; others warn that the benefits are overstated and the risks, particularly to the heart, are real. Every winter there are reports of swimmers who underestimated the cold. I take it seriously. I never swim alone, I never stay in for long, and I never, ever jump.

But I keep coming back. Partly for the shock, which empties your head of everything except the next breath. Partly for the people: the star-jumping pensioner, the weeping Santa, the teenager who brings a flask of hot chocolate to share. Mostly, though, for that moment afterwards, sitting on the bench with my hands wrapped around a cup, when the whole grey city seems to have been switched back on.

----------

Source B: a letter written in 1868 by a young woman on holiday at the seaside to her mother.

My dearest Mamma,

You will be glad to hear that I have at last obeyed Dr Phelps and taken to the sea, though I confess I did so with more terror than obedience.

The bathing machines stand in a long row upon the sands, like little wooden houses that have lost their way. One climbs into the machine, which is very dark and smells strongly of damp straw, and there undresses while a horse drags the whole contraption out into the waves. I was flung about most cruelly. My bonnet struck the wall twice.

When the door was opened, there stood the dipper, a vast woman named Mrs Gant, with arms like a coal-heaver's and a face as red as a boiled ham. Before I could say a word she seized me by both shoulders and plunged me beneath the water three times, very much as one would rinse a stocking. I came up shrieking. The cold was beyond anything I had imagined; it seemed to stop my heart entirely.

Yet I must tell you, Mamma, that when I was returned to the machine and wrapped in my shawl, I felt a glow upon my skin and a lightness in my spirits that I have not known since Papa's illness. Mrs Gant assures me that the sea cures everything from melancholy to the gout, and though I suspect she exaggerates, I am resolved to go again tomorrow.

I beg you not to tell Aunt Lavinia. She believes sea-bathing to be both dangerous and not at all respectable, and I fear she may be right on both counts.

Your loving daughter,
Clara

Use details from both sources. Write a summary of the differences between the writers' experiences of swimming in cold water.

[8 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline (three linked differences, inference from both sources each time):
- Choice and control: the modern writer chooses to swim and manages the risk personally ('I never swim alone... I never, ever jump'), suggesting an adult in control of their own wellbeing. Clara is 'plunged beneath the water three times' by Mrs Gant 'as one would rinse a stocking', implying she has almost no control; her body is handled like laundry.
- Company: Source A's swimmers form a friendly community ('the teenager who brings a flask of hot chocolate to share'), implying the swim is social and supportive. Clara is alone except for a stranger whose job is to dunk her, and she must hide it from 'Aunt Lavinia', which suggests the experience is private, even slightly shameful.
- Reason and attitude: the modern writer swims to recover from a year in which they 'stopped sleeping', and weighs the scientific evidence ('The science is still catching up'), implying a modern, informed approach. Clara goes because a doctor told her to ('obeyed Dr Phelps') and hears Mrs Gant's claim that the sea 'cures everything', implying she relies on authority and folk belief rather than evidence.
- Similarity to avoid labouring: both feel better afterwards ('awake' / 'a lightness in my spirits'), but the modern writer seeks the feeling regularly while Clara is surprised by it.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; perceptive inferences about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts, linked throughout.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some interpretation of differences; attempts at inference; some appropriate references from one or both sources.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple awareness of difference; paraphrase rather than inference; simple references, possibly from one source only.
No credit for analysing language or methods: Q2 rewards what the sources say and imply.

Indicative content: control (self-managed vs dipped by Mrs Gant); company (community of swimmers vs isolation and secrecy); reasons (personal recovery vs doctor's orders); knowledge (scientific caution vs folk claims of cures); equipment and setting (jetty and pond vs bathing machine and horse); attitudes of others (no disapproval mentioned in A vs Aunt Lavinia thinks it 'not at all respectable').
questions.tip: About 8 minutes. Differences in WHAT the sources show, not how they are written. Every point: quotation from A, quotation from B, an inference for each.

How does the writer use language to describe her experience of sea-bathing?

[12 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Tone: comic and self-mocking, but with real feeling underneath. 'with more terror than obedience' uses balanced, witty contrast to set up a humorous account.
- Simile 'like little wooden houses that have lost their way' makes the bathing machines seem absurd and slightly pitiful, revealing a playful eye.
- Sensory detail 'very dark and smells strongly of damp straw' makes the experience unpleasant and confined; 'flung about most cruelly' is hyperbolic, comically dramatic.
- Mrs Gant is a caricature: 'arms like a coal-heaver's' (masculine, working-class strength) and 'a face as red as a boiled ham' (comic, domestic simile). Clara's class position shows in the comparison.
- Verbs 'seized' and 'plunged' show violence and loss of control; the simile 'as one would rinse a stocking' reduces her to an object of laundry, which is both funny and humiliating.
- 'I came up shrieking.' The short sentence captures the shock; 'seemed to stop my heart entirely' is hyperbole but also hints at danger.
- Shift in tone with 'Yet': 'a glow upon my skin and a lightness in my spirits' uses gentle, positive abstract nouns; the reference to 'Papa's illness' reveals the emotional reason the experience matters.
- Ending: irony in 'I fear she may be right on both counts' shows Clara's rebellious humour.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): perceptive, detailed analysis of how the writer's language choices create effects and shape tone and viewpoint; judicious, tightly embedded quotations; sophisticated and accurate subject terminology tied to effect.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clear explanation of the effects of language choices; a relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): some attempt to comment on the effect of language; some appropriate references; some terminology, mostly appropriate.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple comment on effect; simple references; simple terminology, not always accurate.

Indicative content: comic contrast 'more terror than obedience'; personifying simile of the machines; sensory detail; hyperbole 'most cruelly'; caricature similes of Mrs Gant; violent verbs; 'rinse a stocking'; short sentence 'I came up shrieking.'; hyperbole about her heart; tonal turn with 'Yet'; 'glow' and 'lightness'; ironic final line; direct address 'Mamma' creating intimacy.
questions.tip: About 12 minutes. One source only. Track the writer's tone and attitude and analyse how individual words and sentence forms create it.

Compare how the writers convey their different perspectives on swimming in cold water.

In your answer, you could:
- compare their different perspectives
- compare the methods the writers use to convey their perspectives

questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Overview: both writers find cold water frightening and restorative, but the modern writer is a committed, informed enthusiast, while Clara is a reluctant beginner surprised to find herself converted.
- Purpose and audience: A is a public article, so the writer balances personal story with evidence ('Some researchers believe... others warn'), positioning the writer as trustworthy. B is a private letter, so Clara is free to be comic and confiding ('I beg you not to tell Aunt Lavinia').

- Context: in the Victorian period, sea-bathing was often recommended for health, yet some people thought it improper or dangerous (Aunt Lavinia's view), so Clara's enthusiasm is mildly rebellious; today cold swimming is a popular wellbeing trend, so the modern writer's task is to be honest about risk rather than to defend respectability.

Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an extract from a newspaper article written in 1861 about a Saturday night street market in London.

There is no sight in London to equal a street market on a Saturday night, and I would urge any reader who doubts it to walk down the New Cut between the hours of nine and midnight.

The noise is the first thing that strikes one. Every trader bawls his wares at the full stretch of his lungs: 'Here's your fine walnuts, sixteen a penny!' 'Buy, buy, buy!' 'Now's your time for beautiful red herrings!' The din is so tremendous that a man may shout into his companion's ear and not be heard.

The crowd is chiefly made up of the poor, for it is on Saturday that the working man receives his wages, and it is on Saturday night that his wife must make those wages stretch to Sunday's dinner. questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an article from a parenting magazine, written in the 2020s, about children's independence.

When I was nine, my world was roughly a mile wide. I knew every alley, every wall worth climbing, every garden with a dog to avoid. I left the house after breakfast on Saturdays and came back when I was hungry, and nobody, as far as I can remember, ever asked where I had been.

My son is nine now. He has never walked to the end of our road on his own.

I am not proud of this. I tell myself it is the traffic, which is real: the street I played on as a child now carries a lorry every few minutes. I tell myself it is the strangers, though I know, because I have looked it up, that the risk of a child being taken by a stranger is tiny. Mostly, if I am honest, it is the other parents. The fear of being the one who let their child roam, the one the others talk about at the school gate.

And so we have raised a generation of children who are safe, supervised and, according to a growing number of researchers, anxious. Studies suggest that unsupervised play helps children learn to judge risk, solve problems and manage their own emotions. A child who is never allowed to get lost never learns how to find the way home.

Last week, I tried an experiment. I let him walk to the corner shop, three minutes away, with a five-pound note and strict instructions. I watched from the window until he turned the corner, and then I stood in the hallway with my heart going like a drum.

He came back eleven minutes later with a bag of crisps, the wrong change and an expression I had not seen on his face for years. He looked, for want of a better word, enormous.

----------

Source B: an extract from an account written in 1874 by a journalist who visited the poor streets of central London.

In the narrow courts behind Drury Lane, the children are left almost entirely to themselves.

I counted upwards of forty of them in a single yard, not one above twelve years of age, and not one, so far as I could discover, under the eye of any grown person. Their mothers were at the wash-tub or the factory; their fathers, where they had fathers, were at work or at the public-house. The children had the street, and the street had them.

I do not wish to paint too dark a picture. They were, for the most part, merry. A dozen boys had made a cricket bat from a barrel-stave and were playing with tremendous energy against a wicket chalked upon a wall. Girls skipped with a length of old rope, chanting rhymes that I could not follow. One small child, barefoot and very dirty, had appointed herself guardian of a still smaller one and was carrying him about on her hip with the gravity of a duchess.

But I could not watch them without dread. The court is crossed every few minutes by heavy carts, and the drivers do not slacken their pace for children. I was told that two had been killed in that very spot in the past twelvemonth. The gutters run with filth. The language the children use would shame a sailor, and they learn it, as they learn everything, from the street.

These children are not wicked. They are simply unguarded. Every one of them is clever, quick and full of spirit, and every one of them, without school and without care, is in danger of growing into exactly what respectable society most fears. It is not freedom they need. It is someone to look after them.

Use details from both sources. Write a summary of the differences between the children described in the two sources.

[8 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Supervision: the modern son is constantly supervised ('never walked to the end of our road on his own'), implying an overprotected childhood. The Victorian children are 'not one... under the eye of any grown person', implying neglect born of necessity, as their parents are at 'the wash-tub or the factory'.
- Responsibility: in Source B, children take on adult roles: a barefoot girl carries a younger child 'with the gravity of a duchess', suggesting they grow up too fast. In Source A, a three-minute errand is a major event, suggesting modern children are given too little responsibility.
- Confidence and emotion: the modern boy returns 'enormous', implying that independence is new and transformative for him; the Victorian children are already 'merry', 'clever, quick and full of spirit', suggesting confidence that comes from freedom, but at a cost.
- Danger: both face traffic (a lorry 'every few minutes' / carts that 'do not slacken their pace'), but in B the danger is fatal and real ('two had been killed'), while in A it is mostly imagined or social ('the one the others talk about').
- Basic needs: the Victorian children are 'barefoot and very dirty', without school; the modern boy has a five-pound note and comes back with crisps, implying comfort and security.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; perceptive inferences about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts, linked throughout.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some interpretation of differences; attempts at inference; some appropriate references from one or both sources.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple awareness of difference; paraphrase rather than inference; simple references, possibly from one source only.
No credit for analysing language or methods: Q2 rewards what the sources say and imply.

Indicative content: supervised vs unsupervised; protected vs exposed; little responsibility vs adult responsibility (girl carrying the baby); new confidence ('enormous') vs existing spirit ('merry', 'quick'); imagined/social danger vs fatal danger (two killed); comfort vs poverty (barefoot, no school); single child vs crowd of forty.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an extract from a travel book written in 1857 by a woman describing her climb of a mountain in the Alps.

We left the hut at two o'clock in the morning, by the light of a single lantern and beneath a sky so crowded with stars that there seemed scarcely room for one more.

Our party consisted of myself, my brother Henry, and two guides from the village: old Johann and his son Peter, a silent youth of nineteen who carried the greater part of our provisions without the least complaint. I wore a skirt shortened to the ankle, which my brother declared a scandal and which I declared, with equal firmness, a necessity.

For four hours we climbed in darkness over snow so hard that the guides were obliged to cut every step with their axes. The cold was extreme. My fingers lost all feeling within the first hour, and I confess that more than once, clinging to the rope above a slope that fell away into nothing, I wished myself back in my aunt's drawing room with nothing more dangerous before me than the teapot.

Then the dawn came. I cannot hope to describe it properly. The peaks around us caught the light one by one, as though some great hand were lighting candles along an altar, until the whole range blazed rose and gold above a sea of cloud. Henry, who is not a religious man, took off his hat. Old Johann said nothing at all, but I saw him cross himself.

We reached the summit at a little after eight. It was a narrow ridge of snow, no wider than a garden path, and we stood upon it for perhaps a quarter of an hour, entirely alone in the sky. I have been told since that a lady has no business upon a mountain. I can only reply that I have never felt so much in the presence of God, nor so little in need of anybody's permission.

----------

Source B: an extract from a newspaper feature, written in the 2020s, about crowds on Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) in Wales.

At ten past eleven on a Saturday in August, I joined the queue for the summit of Snowdon.

I want to be clear about this. Not a queue for the cafe, or the toilets, or the train. A queue for the top of the highest mountain in Wales. It stretched down the path for roughly a hundred metres, a slow-moving line of walkers in bright waterproofs, and it took me forty minutes to reach the cairn, where I waited a further five while a group of lads in matching T-shirts took it in turns to film themselves.

Hundreds of thousands of people climb Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa, every year. Most of them, on the evidence of that Saturday, come on the same day as me. The paths are worn into deep scars. Litter-pickers report collecting banana skins, drinks cans and, on one memorable occasion, a full-sized inflatable flamingo. Volunteer rescue teams are called out to walkers in trainers who have set off at four in the afternoon with no torch, no map and no idea.

It would be easy to be snobbish about all this, and plenty of people are. But I was struck, too, by how happy everyone was. Families with tiny children on their shoulders. A man in his eighties, climbing it for the fiftieth time. A group of nervous teenagers from Birmingham, none of whom had ever been up a hill before, cheering each other over the last steep section as though they had won a cup final.

The mountain does not belong to the experts. But it cannot survive being loved this much without some help. If we want people to keep feeling what those teenagers felt, we may have to ask them to share it a little more carefully.

Use details from both sources. Write a summary of the differences between the writers' experiences of reaching the summit.

[8 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Solitude vs crowds: the 1857 writer stands on the ridge 'entirely alone in the sky', implying a private, almost sacred experience. The modern writer must 'queue' for forty minutes and wait while lads 'film themselves', implying the summit has become a crowded, public stage.
- Effort and danger: the Victorian party climbs for hours in darkness, with guides cutting 'every step', implying real danger and achievement. The modern writer's main obstacle is other people; the danger described belongs to unprepared walkers 'in trainers'.
- Feeling at the top: A feels 'in the presence of God', implying spiritual awe; B's strongest emotion is surprise at 'how happy everyone was', implying joy that is shared and social rather than private.
- Who is there: A's party is small and select (a lady, her brother, two guides), implying mountaineering is for a privileged few. B describes families, an eighty-year-old and teenagers from Birmingham, implying the mountain is now open to everyone.
- Gender: the 1857 writer faces disapproval ('a lady has no business upon a mountain'); no one in B questions who belongs, except the 'snobbish'.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): perceptive synthesis of both sources; perceptive inferences about the differences; judicious quotations from both texts, linked throughout.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): clear synthesis of both sources; clear inferences; relevant quotations from both texts.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): some interpretation of differences; attempts at inference; some appropriate references from one or both sources.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple awareness of difference; paraphrase rather than inference; simple references, possibly from one source only.
No credit for analysing language or methods: Q2 rewards what the sources say and imply.

Indicative content: alone vs queuing; danger and skill vs overcrowding and litter; spiritual awe vs shared happiness; small privileged party vs mass public; summit at about 8am after six hours of climbing vs 11am Saturday; gender disapproval in A; damage to the mountain only in B.
questions.tip: About 8 minutes. Differences in WHAT the sources show, not how they are written. Every point: quotation from A, quotation from B, an inference for each.

How does the writer use language to describe the crowds on Snowdon?

[12 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Tone: wry and amused at first, then thoughtful and fair-minded.
- 'I want to be clear about this.' The direct address and emphatic statement set up the absurdity; the negated list of three 'Not a queue for the cafe, or the toilets, or the train.' builds comic disbelief before 'A queue for the top of the highest mountain in Wales.'
- Precise numbers ('ten past eleven', 'roughly a hundred metres', 'forty minutes', 'a further five') make the crowding concrete and make the waiting feel endless.
- 'a slow-moving line of walkers in bright waterproofs' paints the queue like a procession; the 'lads in matching T-shirts' filming themselves is gently mocking.
- The metaphor 'worn into deep scars' personifies the mountain as wounded, introducing the cost of crowds.
- Bathos: the list 'banana skins, drinks cans and... a full-sized inflatable flamingo' ends with an absurd item for comic effect while making a serious point about litter.
- The tricolon 'no torch, no map and no idea' is humorous but critical of unprepared walkers.
- Turn: 'It would be easy to be snobbish' shows self-awareness; the list of minor sentences ('Families with tiny children on their shoulders. A man in his eighties...') builds a warm, inclusive picture.
- Simile 'as though they had won a cup final' celebrates ordinary, everyday joy.
- Ending: 'loved this much' personifies the mountain as something fragile; the modal 'may have to' and gentle 'a little more carefully' show a balanced, persuasive conclusion.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): perceptive, detailed analysis of how the writer's language choices create effects and shape tone and viewpoint; judicious, tightly embedded quotations; sophisticated and accurate subject terminology tied to effect.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clear explanation of the effects of language choices; a relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): some attempt to comment on the effect of language; some appropriate references; some terminology, mostly appropriate.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple comment on effect; simple references; simple terminology, not always accurate.

questions.answer:

Paper 2 Question 2

You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Source A: an article from a newspaper website, written in the 2020s, about cold-water swimming in London.

The thermometer on the jetty says four degrees. I have learned not to look at it.

It is seven in the morning on Hampstead Heath, the sky the colour of wet newspaper, and there are already eleven of us queuing on the wooden boards in dressing gowns and woolly hats. Nobody talks much. One woman, who tells me she is seventy-three, is doing star jumps. A man in a Santa hat is quietly weeping, though he insists this is 'just the wind'.

I started cold-water swimming two winters ago, after a year in which I had stopped sleeping, stopped running and very nearly stopped leaving the house. A friend dragged me here. I lasted forty seconds and swore, loudly and inventively, for all of them. Then I climbed out, shaking and scarlet, and felt something I had not felt in months: awake.

The science is still catching up. Some researchers believe cold water may lift mood and reduce inflammation; others warn that the benefits are overstated and the risks, particularly to the heart, are real. Every winter there are reports of swimmers who underestimated the cold. I take it seriously. I never swim alone, I never stay in for long, and I never, ever jump.

But I keep coming back. Partly for the shock, which empties your head of everything except the next breath. Partly for the people: the star-jumping pensioner, the weeping Santa, the teenager who brings a flask of hot chocolate to share. Mostly, though, for that moment afterwards, sitting on the bench with my hands wrapped around a cup, when the whole grey city seems to have been switched back on.

----------

Source B: a letter written in 1868 by a young woman on holiday at the seaside to her mother.

My dearest Mamma,

You will be glad to hear that I have at last obeyed Dr Phelps and taken to the sea, though I confess I did so with more terror than obedience.

The bathing machines stand in a long row upon the sands, like little wooden houses that have lost their way. One climbs into the machine, which is very dark and smells strongly of damp straw, and there undresses while a horse drags the whole contraption out into the waves. I was flung about most cruelly. My bonnet struck the wall twice.

When the door was opened, there stood the dipper, a vast woman named Mrs Gant, with arms like a coal-heaver's and a face as red as a boiled ham. Before I could say a word she seized me by both shoulders and plunged me beneath the water three times, very much as one would rinse a stocking. I came up shrieking. The cold was beyond anything I had imagined; it seemed to stop my heart entirely.

Yet I must tell you, Mamma, that when I was returned to the machine and wrapped in my shawl, I felt a glow upon my skin and a lightness in my spirits that I have not known since Papa's illness. Mrs Gant assures me that the sea cures everything from melancholy to the gout, and though I suspect she exaggerates, I am resolved to go again tomorrow.

I beg you not to tell Aunt Lavinia. She believes sea-bathing to be both dangerous and not at all respectable, and I fear she may be right on both counts.

Your loving daughter,
Clara

Use details from both sources. Write a summary of the differences between the people the writers meet when they swim.

[8 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Equals vs servant: the modern writer's companions are fellow swimmers, a 'star-jumping pensioner' and a 'weeping Santa', implying an equal, friendly community. Clara's only companion is Mrs Gant, 'the dipper', whose job is to plunge her, implying a relationship of payment and class.
- Support vs force: the teenager 'who brings a flask of hot chocolate to share' suggests kindness; Mrs Gant 'seized me by both shoulders', suggesting physical domination, even if well meant.
- Attitudes to the cold: the modern swimmers cope with humour (the man insists his tears are 'just the wind'); Mrs Gant is confident that the sea 'cures everything', implying unquestioning belief.
- Disapproving others: Clara must hide the swim from 'Aunt Lavinia', implying that her wider social circle disapproves; nothing suggests the modern writer faces such judgement.

Level 2 (3-4 marks): some interpretation of differences; attempts at inference; some appropriate references from one or both sources.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple awareness of difference; paraphrase rather than inference; simple references, possibly from one source only.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Homework is a waste of time. Schools should ban it and let young people use their evenings to rest, work or follow their own interests.'

Write an article for a national newspaper in which you argue for or against this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan (nuanced: against a ban, for reform):
Headline: 'Don't Ban Homework. Fix It.'
Strapline: a Year 11 student on why the problem is not homework but busywork.
1. Hook: anecdote of 11pm, a worksheet on colouring a map, a mock exam the next morning.
2. Concede the problem: tiredness, part-time jobs, caring responsibilities; not every home has a quiet desk.
3. Turn: retrieval practice and past papers work; independent study is what separates grades.
4. Counter-argument rebutted: 'young people need rest'. Agreed: so set less, but make it count.
5. Proposal: three rules for good homework (short, purposeful, marked).
6. Ending: return to the map worksheet; call to action to heads and teachers.

Sample opening:
It is eleven o'clock on a Tuesday night and I am colouring in a map. Not revising for tomorrow's maths mock. Not sleeping. Colouring, with a felt tip that is running out, a map of a country I already know the shape of, because a worksheet told me to. If you want to understand why so many teenagers hate homework, start there.
ms: Content and organisation, Level 4 (19-24 marks): compelling, convincing communication; tone, style and register skilfully matched to audience and purpose; extensive, ambitious vocabulary used precisely; deliberately crafted linguistic devices; varied, inventive structure; fully developed ideas in fluently linked paragraphs.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Zoos are cruel and old-fashioned. In the twenty-first century, there is no good reason to keep wild animals in captivity.'

Write a speech to be delivered at a debate held by a local wildlife charity in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. Address the audience: 'Good evening, everyone.' Open with an image: a polar bear pacing the same eight steps.
2. Concede what is wrong with bad zoos: small enclosures, stress behaviours, animals as entertainment.
3. Turn: modern conservation zoos and breeding programmes; species that survive today partly because of captive breeding.
4. Counter-argument: 'protect them in the wild instead'. Rebut: we should do both; habitats are shrinking faster than we can protect them.
5. Vision: zoos as arks, not prisons; three conditions they must meet.
6. Ending: return to the pacing bear; a rhetorical question to the audience; 'The choice is not between zoos and freedom. It is between zoos and extinction.'

Sample opening:
Good evening, everyone. Eight steps. Turn. Eight steps. Turn. That was the polar bear I watched as a child, walking the same short path along the edge of his concrete pool, hour after hour, until I asked my dad if he was lost. I have never forgotten him. And I want to start tonight by saying, clearly, that the people who call zoos cruel are sometimes right.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Young people today spend too much time on their phones. Parents should take control and limit their children's screen time.'

Write a letter to the editor of your local newspaper in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
Letter conventions: your address (or 'Dear Editor'), formal register, 'Yours faithfully'.
1. State purpose and stance: respond to a recent article; argue that limits work best when agreed, not imposed.
2. Acknowledge the problem: sleep, focus, comparison culture.
3. Argue against simple parental control: teenagers find workarounds; trust breaks down; phones are also how we study, keep in touch, stay safe.
4. Alternative: family agreements, phone-free meals, phones out of bedrooms at night for everyone, including adults.
5. Ending: a reasonable, persuasive appeal to parents.

Sample opening:
Dear Editor,
I am writing in response to last week's article, 'Unplug Our Children', which argued that parents should simply take their teenagers' phones away. As a sixteen-year-old who has, I admit, checked my phone twice while writing this paragraph, I agree that there is a problem. I do not agree that confiscation is the answer.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Fast fashion is destroying the planet. It is time we stopped buying cheap clothes we do not need.'

Write an essay for an online magazine in which you explain your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan (explanatory essay with a clear thesis):
Title: 'The True Cost of a Five-Pound T-Shirt'
1. Introduction: an image of a haul video; thesis: fast fashion's price is paid elsewhere, but blame should not fall only on teenagers with little money.
2. Environmental cost: water use, waste, clothes worn a handful of times then binned. Keep facts general and plausible rather than inventing precise statistics.
3. Human cost: garment workers, low pay, unsafe factories.
4. Complication: for people on low incomes, cheap clothes are a necessity; the problem is overconsumption, not affordability.
5. Solutions: buying less and better, second-hand and swapping, repairing, pressure on brands.
6. Conclusion: return to the haul; reframe it as a choice about value.

Sample opening:
In a video with two million views, a girl not much older than me pulls thirty items of clothing from a single plastic bag. Each one is held up to the camera, praised for exactly four seconds, and tossed onto a growing pile on her bed. It is cheerful, harmless-looking and, if you stop to think about where those clothes came from and where they will end up, quietly horrifying.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Sport is far too important to be cut from the school timetable. Every student should do at least five hours of PE a week.'

Write a letter to your headteacher in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
'Dear Mr/Ms [name]' and 'Yours sincerely'.
1. Purpose: respond to the plan to reduce PE to make room for exam revision.
2. Argue for more PE but not necessarily five hours of team sport: physical health, mental health, focus and behaviour in lessons.
3. Counter-argument: exam pressure, timetable limits. Rebut: exercise improves concentration; a tired, stressed Year 11 does not revise well.
4. Address the students PE puts off: offer choice (dance, gym, yoga, walking), so that 'sport' includes everyone.
5. Proposal: a realistic compromise (three hours timetabled plus clubs) and an offer to help.
6. Ending: polite, firm request for a meeting or a student survey.

Sample opening:
Dear Mrs Patel,
I am writing on behalf of many students in Year 11 about the proposal to reduce our PE lessons in order to make more time for revision. I understand why the idea was suggested. Our exams matter, and nobody knows that better than we do. However, I want to explain why cutting the one hour in the day when we stop sitting still could make our results worse, not better.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Celebrities and influencers are terrible role models for young people. We should stop paying attention to them.'

Write a speech for a school assembly in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
[40 marks]

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.
questions.answer:
Level 4 plan:
1. Opening: address the audience ('Morning, Year 9, 10 and 11'); a rhetorical question: 'Who did you look at first today?'
2. Concede: filters, unrealistic bodies and lifestyles, adverts disguised as friendship, toxic behaviour rewarded with clicks.
3. Complicate: some celebrities use their platform well (campaigns on free school meals, mental health, racism); influence is a tool, not a crime.
4. Key argument: the problem is passive scrolling, not attention. Choose your role models deliberately.
5. Practical challenge: three questions to ask before following someone.
6. Ending: return to the opening question; a memorable final line ('Follow people who make you bigger, not smaller.').

Sample opening:
Morning, everyone. Quick question, and be honest, because nobody is checking: who was the first person you looked at today? Not your mum. Not your brother. I mean the first face on your screen. For most of us, it was someone we have never met, who does not know we exist, and who is, right now, being paid to make us want something.

Paper 2 Question 5 (40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy)

'Libraries are a thing of the past. Everything you need is online, so councils should close them and spend the money elsewhere.'

Write a letter to your local council in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)

Spend about 45 minutes on this question.

Level 4 plan:
'Dear Sir or Madam' and 'Yours faithfully'.
1. Purpose: object to the proposed closure of the local library.
2. Not everything is online: not every home has fast internet, a laptop or a quiet space to work.
3. The library as a community hub: toddlers' story time, older people, job seekers using computers, students revising after school.

I am writing to object, in the strongest terms, to the council's proposal to close Ward's Corner Library. I understand that the council faces difficult choices. options: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to complain about influencers.
Morning, everyone. Quick question, and be honest: who was the first face you saw on your screen today?
Influencers are people who post things online and some of them have lots of followers.
In this speech I will talk about why influencers are bad.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 5: which sentence shows the most sophisticated handling of a counter-argument?
options: Of course, some people think zoos are good.
Some people disagree but they are wrong.
Critics are right that some zoos are little more than prisons; but to close every zoo because of the worst of them is to abandon the species that only survive because of the best.
There are two sides to every argument and both are important.
ms: C concedes a fair point precisely, then turns it with a balanced antithesis that strengthens the writer's own case.
questions.tip: Concede, then counter: 'Critics are right that... but...'. Dismissing the other side ('they are wrong') reads as weak.

A story about a character with an opinion
A purely factual report with no opinion
