questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3

You now need to refer only to Source B.

Source B: an article from a newspaper website, written in the 2020s, about cold-water swimming in London.

The thermometer on the jetty says four degrees. I have learned not to look at it.

It is seven in the morning on Hampstead Heath, the sky the colour of wet newspaper, and there are already eleven of us queuing on the wooden boards in dressing gowns and woolly hats. Nobody talks much. One woman, who tells me she is seventy-three, is doing star jumps. A man in a Santa hat is quietly weeping, though he insists this is 'just the wind'.

I started cold-water swimming two winters ago, after a year in which I had stopped sleeping, stopped running and very nearly stopped leaving the house. A friend dragged me here. I lasted forty seconds and swore, loudly and inventively, for all of them. Then I climbed out, shaking and scarlet, and felt something I had not felt in months: awake.

The science is still catching up. Some researchers believe cold water may lift mood and reduce inflammation; others warn that the benefits are overstated and the risks, particularly to the heart, are real. Every winter there are reports of swimmers who underestimated the cold. I take it seriously. I never swim alone, I never stay in for long, and I never, ever jump.

But I keep coming back. Partly for the shock, which empties your head of everything except the next breath. Partly for the people: the star-jumping pensioner, the weeping Santa, the teenager who brings a flask of hot chocolate to share. Mostly, though, for that moment afterwards, sitting on the bench with my hands wrapped around a cup, when the whole grey city seems to have been switched back on.

How does the writer use language to present their experience of cold-water swimming?

[12 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Tone: wry, self-deprecating and honest, moving to warmth and gratitude.
- Opening: the short declarative 'The thermometer on the jetty says four degrees.' followed by 'I have learned not to look at it.' creates humour and implies a fear they have learned to manage.
- Simile 'the colour of wet newspaper' is a grey, urban, slightly comic image that sets the bleak scene.
- Comic detail of the people: 'A man in a Santa hat is quietly weeping, though he insists this is "just the wind".' The juxtaposition of festive costume and tears is funny and humane.
- Tricolon with repetition 'stopped sleeping, stopped running and very nearly stopped leaving the house' builds a sense of a life shrinking, with 'very nearly' adding understated seriousness.
- 'swore, loudly and inventively, for all of them' is comic hyperbole; the paired adverbs show the writer's humour.
- 'shaking and scarlet' pairs two physical signs of shock; the colon before the single word 'awake' isolates it as a revelation.
- Balanced, cautious language in the science paragraph ('may', 'believe', 'warn') shows honesty; the triple 'I never... I never... I never, ever jump' stresses discipline.
- Ending: anaphora 'Partly... Partly... Mostly' structures the writer's reasons; the metaphor of the city 'switched back on' links the writer's own recovery to the world around her, a hopeful final image.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): perceptive, detailed analysis of how the writer's language choices create effects and shape tone and viewpoint; judicious, tightly embedded quotations; sophisticated and accurate subject terminology tied to effect.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clear explanation of the effects of language choices; a relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): some attempt to comment on the effect of language; some appropriate references; some terminology, mostly appropriate.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple comment on effect; simple references; simple terminology, not always accurate.

Indicative content: short declaratives and humour; simile 'wet newspaper'; comic juxtaposition of the Santa hat; tricolon of 'stopped'; hyperbole 'loudly and inventively'; paired adjectives 'shaking and scarlet'; colon and isolated 'awake'; modal verbs of caution; repetition of 'never'; anaphora of 'Partly'; final metaphor 'switched back on'.
questions.tip: About 12 minutes. One source only. Track the writer's tone and attitude and analyse how individual words and sentence forms create it.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3

You now need to refer only to Source B.

Source B: an extract from a newspaper article written in 1861 about a Saturday night street market in London.

There is no sight in London to equal a street market on a Saturday night, and I would urge any reader who doubts it to walk down the New Cut between the hours of nine and midnight.

The noise is the first thing that strikes one. Every trader bawls his wares at the full stretch of his lungs: 'Here's your fine walnuts, sixteen a penny!' 'Buy, buy, buy!' 'Now's your time for beautiful red herrings!' The din is so tremendous that a man may shout into his companion's ear and not be heard.

Then there are the lights. Every stall has its own, so that the street is lit by a hundred flames of every description: the gas-lamps of the butcher, the grease-lamps of the fishmonger, the candles stuck in turnips upon the barrow of the potato-man. The whole scene flickers like a dream of fire.

The crowd is chiefly made up of the poor, for it is on Saturday that the working man receives his wages, and it is on Saturday night that his wife must make those wages stretch to Sunday's dinner. I watched one such woman, thin and pale, with an infant wrapped in her shawl, examine a single cabbage for fully five minutes before she bought it. She counted out her coins three times. I do not think I have ever seen money handled so tenderly.

It is the fashion among respectable people to call these markets a nuisance and to demand that the police clear them away. I can only say that, for the thousands who depend upon them, they are not a nuisance but a necessity. Close them, and you do not remove the poverty; you merely remove the bread.

How does the writer use language to describe the market and the people who shop there?

[12 marks]
questions.answer:
Level 4 outline:
- Tone: enthusiastic and vivid, then compassionate and finally indignant.
- Opening superlative 'There is no sight in London to equal' and imperative 'I would urge any reader' establish authority and enthusiasm.
- Direct speech from traders ('Buy, buy, buy!') recreates the noise, making the reader hear the market; the repetition is comic and energetic.
- Hyperbole 'a man may shout into his companion's ear and not be heard' stresses the overwhelming din.
- Listing of lamps ('the gas-lamps of the butcher, the grease-lamps of the fishmonger, the candles stuck in turnips') creates abundance and shows inventive poverty; the simile 'flickers like a dream of fire' makes the scene magical and unreal.
- Shift to the poor: 'thin and pale' adjectives evoke sympathy; the precise detail 'fully five minutes' and 'counted out her coins three times' show anxiety and care.
- 'I do not think I have ever seen money handled so tenderly.' The adverb 'tenderly' transforms money into something precious, giving dignity to poverty.
- Final paragraph: ironic 'respectable people' criticises the middle classes; antithesis 'not a nuisance but a necessity' (with alliteration) and the balanced aphorism 'you do not remove the poverty; you merely remove the bread' end with moral force.
ms: Level 4 (10-12 marks): perceptive, detailed analysis of how the writer's language choices create effects and shape tone and viewpoint; judicious, tightly embedded quotations; sophisticated and accurate subject terminology tied to effect.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): clear explanation of the effects of language choices; a relevant range of quotations; accurate subject terminology.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): some attempt to comment on the effect of language; some appropriate references; some terminology, mostly appropriate.
Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple comment on effect; simple references; simple terminology, not always accurate.

Indicative content: superlative opening; imperative; direct speech and repetition; hyperbole of noise; listing of lamps; simile 'like a dream of fire'; adjectives 'thin and pale'; precise numbers; adverb 'tenderly'; irony in 'respectable'; antithesis; alliteration 'nuisance... necessity'; semicolon-balanced aphorism.
questions.tip: About 12 minutes. One source only. Track the writer's tone and attitude and analyse how individual words and sentence forms create it.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: a letter written in 1868 by a young woman on holiday at the seaside to her mother.

The bathing machines stand in a long row upon the sands, like little wooden houses that have lost their way. One climbs into the machine, which is very dark and smells strongly of damp straw, and there undresses while a horse drags the whole contraption out into the waves. I was flung about most cruelly. My bonnet struck the wall twice.

When the door was opened, there stood the dipper, a vast woman named Mrs Gant, with arms like a coal-heaver's and a face as red as a boiled ham. Before I could say a word she seized me by both shoulders and plunged me beneath the water three times, very much as one would rinse a stocking. I came up shrieking. The cold was beyond anything I had imagined; it seemed to stop my heart entirely.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: Clara's bonnet struck the wall three times
Mrs Gant asked Clara's permission before dipping her
The bathing machine smelled of fresh hay
A horse dragged the bathing machine into the waves
ms: 'while a horse drags the whole contraption out into the waves'. The smell is 'damp straw', the bonnet struck the wall twice, and Mrs Gant seized her 'Before I could say a word'.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: a post from a food blog, written in the 2020s, about a street-food market in south London.

Every Friday from April to October, a multi-storey car park in south London becomes the best restaurant in the city. You climb six flights of concrete stairs that smell faintly of rain and, honestly, something worse, and then you push through a fire door and the whole of London is suddenly spread out in front of you, glittering, while forty food stalls fill the air with smoke.

I have been coming for three years and I have still not eaten everything. Last week it was Nigerian suya: beef skewers rolled in spice so hot it made my eyes stream, served in folded paper with raw onion and a cheerful warning from the man at the grill. Before that, Korean fried chicken, Venezuelan arepas, a doughnut filled with custard so rich I had to sit down.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The market runs every Friday all year round
The writer climbs six flights of stairs to reach it
The suya was served on a plastic plate
ms: 'You climb six flights of concrete stairs'. It runs April to October, there are forty stalls, and the suya came 'in folded paper'.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: an extract from an account written in 1874 by a journalist who visited the poor streets of central London.

I counted upwards of forty of them in a single yard, not one above twelve years of age, and not one, so far as I could discover, under the eye of any grown person. Their mothers were at the wash-tub or the factory; their fathers, where they had fathers, were at work or at the public-house. The children had the street, and the street had them.

I do not wish to paint too dark a picture. They were, for the most part, merry. A dozen boys had made a cricket bat from a barrel-stave and were playing with tremendous energy against a wicket chalked upon a wall. Girls skipped with a length of old rope, chanting rhymes that I could not follow. One small child, barefoot and very dirty, had appointed herself guardian of a still smaller one and was carrying him about on her hip with the gravity of a duchess.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The girls' rhymes were easy for the writer to follow
The boys' cricket bat was made from a barrel-stave
The writer counted fewer than forty children
ms: 'made a cricket bat from a barrel-stave'. He counted 'upwards of forty', could not follow the rhymes, and says they were 'for the most part, merry'.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: an extract from a newspaper feature, written in the 2020s, about crowds on Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) in Wales.

I want to be clear about this. Not a queue for the cafe, or the toilets, or the train. A queue for the top of the highest mountain in Wales. It stretched down the path for roughly a hundred metres, a slow-moving line of walkers in bright waterproofs, and it took me forty minutes to reach the cairn, where I waited a further five while a group of lads in matching T-shirts took it in turns to film themselves.

Hundreds of thousands of people climb Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa, every year. Most of them, on the evidence of that Saturday, come on the same day as me. The paths are worn into deep scars. Litter-pickers report collecting banana skins, drinks cans and, on one memorable occasion, a full-sized inflatable flamingo. Volunteer rescue teams are called out to walkers in trainers who have set off at four in the afternoon with no torch, no map and no idea.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: It took the writer forty-five minutes in total from joining the queue to finishing their wait at the cairn
The queue stretched for about a kilometre
The lads in matching T-shirts filmed the writer
The queue was for the summit cafe
ms: Forty minutes to reach the cairn plus 'a further five' = 45 minutes. The queue was for the summit, the lads filmed themselves, and it was 'roughly a hundred metres'.
questions.tip: Some true statements need you to put two details together. Check the arithmetic and the exact wording.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: an extract from a travel book written in 1857 by a woman describing her climb of a mountain in the Alps.

For four hours we climbed in darkness over snow so hard that the guides were obliged to cut every step with their axes. The cold was extreme. My fingers lost all feeling within the first hour, and I confess that more than once, clinging to the rope above a slope that fell away into nothing, I wished myself back in my aunt's drawing room with nothing more dangerous before me than the teapot.

Then the dawn came. I cannot hope to describe it properly. The peaks around us caught the light one by one, as though some great hand were lighting candles along an altar, until the whole range blazed rose and gold above a sea of cloud. Henry, who is not a religious man, took off his hat. Old Johann said nothing at all, but I saw him cross himself.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The writer's fingers lost all feeling within the first hour
The climb in darkness lasted about two hours
The guides used ropes to cut the steps
The writer never wished she were somewhere else
ms: 'My fingers lost all feeling within the first hour'. The climb lasted four hours, she wished herself back in the drawing room, and the steps were cut with axes.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: an article from a parenting magazine, written in the 2020s, about children's independence.

I am not proud of this. I tell myself it is the traffic, which is real: the street I played on as a child now carries a lorry every few minutes. I tell myself it is the strangers, though I know, because I have looked it up, that the risk of a child being taken by a stranger is tiny. Mostly, if I am honest, it is the other parents. The fear of being the one who let their child roam, the one the others talk about at the school gate.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The writer says the risk of a child being taken by a stranger is tiny
The writer's street has no traffic
The writer is proud of how they treat their son
The writer does not care what other parents think
ms: 'the risk of a child being taken by a stranger is tiny'. The writer is 'not proud', the street carries 'a lorry every few minutes', and fear of other parents is the main reason.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 1 practice.

Source A: an extract from a newspaper article written in 1861 about a Saturday night street market in London.

Then there are the lights. Every stall has its own, so that the street is lit by a hundred flames of every description: the gas-lamps of the butcher, the grease-lamps of the fishmonger, the candles stuck in turnips upon the barrow of the potato-man. The whole scene flickers like a dream of fire.

The crowd is chiefly made up of the poor, for it is on Saturday that the working man receives his wages, and it is on Saturday night that his wife must make those wages stretch to Sunday's dinner. I watched one such woman, thin and pale, with an infant wrapped in her shawl, examine a single cabbage for fully five minutes before she bought it. She counted out her coins three times. I do not think I have ever seen money handled so tenderly.

Which statement is TRUE according to this part of Source A?
options: The potato-man used candles stuck in turnips
Only the butcher's stall had a light
The working man is paid on Friday
ms: 'the candles stuck in turnips upon the barrow of the potato-man'. Every stall had a light, she bought a single cabbage, and wages come on Saturday.
questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Check every statement against the exact words. Distractors change one detail (a number, a time, a feeling).

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 2: which assessment objective does this question test?
options: AO1: identify and interpret information, and select and synthesise evidence from different texts
ms: Q2 is AO1 synthesis and inference. Methods (AO2/AO3) are not rewarded here.
questions.tip: If you catch yourself naming a technique in Q2, cut it and write an inference instead.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2 practice. Source A (2020s) describes swimmers on Hampstead Heath sharing hot chocolate; Source B (1868) describes Clara being plunged under the water by a dipper called Mrs Gant.

Which sentence would be credited most highly in a summary of differences about the people the writers meet?
options: The modern swimmers form a community of equals, with a teenager bringing hot chocolate 'to share', whereas Clara's only companion is a paid dipper who 'seized' her, implying a relationship of class and force rather than friendship.
Both sources are about swimming in cold water.
In Source A there are swimmers and in Source B there is Mrs Gant.
Source A uses humour, while Source B uses similes such as 'a face as red as a boiled ham'.
ms: B gives a difference, embeds evidence from both sources and makes an inference. A analyses methods; C only paraphrases; D is a similarity.
questions.tip: Point of difference + quotation from each + 'implying/suggesting'. That is the Q2 formula.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 2: a student writes three paragraphs about Source A, then two about Source B, with no links between them. What is the main weakness?
options: They did not include enough techniques
They should have written about similarities
The response does not synthesise; differences must be drawn out by linking the sources point by point
ms: Synthesis means bringing details from both sources together. Separate accounts limit the response to the lower levels.
questions.tip: Use comparative connectives in every paragraph: whereas, by contrast, unlike.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 2 practice. Source A (1861): the poor buy food with that day's wages 'to stretch to Sunday's dinner'. Source B (2020s): 'a cocktail will set you back twelve' pounds.

Which inference best explains the difference?
options: The modern writer does not like cocktails
The Victorian market exists to help people survive, while the modern market is a place of leisure for people with money to spare
ms: B is a supported inference about purpose. A is a similarity; C and D are unsupported.
questions.tip: An inference goes one step beyond the quotation: what does this detail tell you about the people or the place?

questions.q: Question 2 practice: which sentence shows the most perceptive Question 2 point about the two sources?
options: Source A is modern and Source B is old.
While both writers feel better after the cold, the modern writer seeks that feeling deliberately, whereas Clara is surprised by it.
ms: Identifying a shared idea and then a difference within it shows perceptive synthesis, a Level 4 feature.
questions.tip: Higher-level Q2 answers often find the difference inside a similarity.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3 practice.

Source B: an extract from a newspaper feature, written in the 2020s, about crowds on Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) in Wales.

Hundreds of thousands of people climb Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa, every year. Most of them, on the evidence of that Saturday, come on the same day as me. The paths are worn into deep scars. Litter-pickers report collecting banana skins, drinks cans and, on one memorable occasion, a full-sized inflatable flamingo. Volunteer rescue teams are called out to walkers in trainers who have set off at four in the afternoon with no torch, no map and no idea.

Which technique creates comic effect at the end of the list of litter?
options: Bathos: the list ends with an absurd item, 'a full-sized inflatable flamingo'
ms: A serious list of litter drops into an absurd final item, which is bathos (anticlimax for comic effect).
questions.tip: Name the technique and then explain the tone it creates: here, humour that still makes a serious point about litter.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3 practice.

Source B: an extract from an account written in 1874 by a journalist who visited the poor streets of central London.

I counted upwards of forty of them in a single yard, not one above twelve years of age, and not one, so far as I could discover, under the eye of any grown person. Their mothers were at the wash-tub or the factory; their fathers, where they had fathers, were at work or at the public-house. The children had the street, and the street had them.

Which comment best analyses 'The children had the street, and the street had them.'?
options: It is a compound sentence with the conjunction 'and'.
It shows the children like playing in the street.
It is a simile comparing children to a street.
The chiasmus reverses the words so that the street shifts from something the children own to something that owns them, suggesting their freedom is also a trap.
ms: B names the device (chiasmus: an inverted, mirrored structure) and explores the double meaning. C is accurate but has no effect; D is literal.
questions.tip: Level 4 language answers explore how a structure changes meaning, not just what it is called.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3 practice.

Source B: an extract from a newspaper article written in 1861 about a Saturday night street market in London.

It is the fashion among respectable people to call these markets a nuisance and to demand that the police clear them away. I can only say that, for the thousands who depend upon them, they are not a nuisance but a necessity. Close them, and you do not remove the poverty; you merely remove the bread.

Which word best describes the writer's tone here?
ms: The writer attacks the 'respectable people' and argues forcefully: indignant (angry at something unjust).
questions.tip: Learn precise tone words: indignant, wry, scathing, earnest, sardonic, ambivalent.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 3: how many sources should you write about?
options: Only the one named in the question
ms: Q3 directs you to one source only. Writing about the other source earns nothing.
questions.tip: Check which source the question names before you start: in AQA papers it is Source B.

questions.q:
Paper 2 Question 3 practice.

Source B: an article from a newspaper website, written in the 2020s, about cold-water swimming in London.

I started cold-water swimming two winters ago, after a year in which I had stopped sleeping, stopped running and very nearly stopped leaving the house. A friend dragged me here. I lasted forty seconds and swore, loudly and inventively, for all of them. Then I climbed out, shaking and scarlet, and felt something I had not felt in months: awake.

Which comment best analyses the writer's use of the colon in the final sentence?
options: The colon shows the writer is tired.
The colon creates a pause that isolates the single word 'awake', presenting it as a sudden revelation and suggesting the swim brought them back to life after months of numbness.
ms: B explains how punctuation shapes the effect and links it to the writer's experience. Punctuation is part of language analysis when you explain its effect.
questions.tip: Sentence forms and punctuation count as language in Q3. Analyse them when they do something striking.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 4: which assessment objective does this question test?
options: AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed
ms: Q4 on Paper 2 is the only AO3 question: perspectives plus methods, across both sources.
questions.tip: Two things in every paragraph: what each writer thinks and how they show it.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 4: which sentence best compares methods as well as perspectives?
options: Source A was written in the 2020s.
Source A likes freedom and Source B does not.

The writers end very differently: the modern parent's single word 'enormous' celebrates independence, while the journalist's antithesis 'It is not freedom they need' rejects it, so their endings directly oppose each other.
Source B uses lots of adjectives.
ms: B compares perspective AND method (endings, single word vs antithesis) with evidence from both sources.
questions.tip: A Q4 paragraph that names no methods cannot get beyond the lower levels.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 4: how should context be used?
options: Write a separate paragraph of history about the Victorian era
Briefly explain why a perspective differs (era, purpose, audience) and link it straight back to the text
Only mention the dates of the sources
ms: Context helps explain WHY perspectives differ, a Level 4 feature, but it must stay short and tied to the writers' words.
questions.tip: One sentence of context, linked to a quotation, is worth more than a paragraph of history.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 4: how long should you spend on this question?
ms: 16 marks; about 20 minutes. It needs both whole sources.
questions.tip: Leave a full 45 minutes for Q5 afterwards: Q5 is worth 40 marks.

questions.q: Paper 2 Question 4 practice. Source A (1857): 'I have never felt so much in the presence of God'. Source B (2020s): teenagers cheering 'as though they had won a cup final'. What is the most perceptive comparison?
options: Both writers describe joy at the summit, but A's is solitary and spiritual, expressed through religious language, while B's is collective and everyday, expressed through a sporting simile, which reflects a shift from mountains as sacred places for a few to shared spaces for many.
Source A is religious and Source B is about football.
Source B is funnier than Source A.
ms: B compares perspectives, names methods and explains the wider significance (who mountains belong to).
questions.tip: The best comparisons find a shared idea, then show how the writers treat it differently and why.

questions.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
ms: A sentence-starting adverbial such as 'However' is followed by a comma.
questions.tip: When 'however' joins two main clauses, use a semicolon before it: 'I was tired; however, I stayed.'

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'who's' or 'whose'?
options: The boy who's coat was red ran off.
The girl whose phone was stolen called the police.
ms: 'Whose' shows possession; 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has'.
questions.tip: Test by expanding: if 'who is' fits, use who's.

questions.q: Which sentence avoids a run-on (fused) sentence?
options: The bus was late so, I missed my exam.
The bus was late I missed my exam.
The bus was late, so I missed my exam.
The bus was late, I missed my exam.
ms: Two main clauses need a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction ('so').
questions.tip: Run-ons and comma splices are the most common AO6 error at grades 5-6. Proofread for them.

questions.q: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The list of names were pinned to the door.
The list of names have been pinned to the door.
The lists of names was pinned to the door.
The list of names was pinned to the door.
ms: The subject is 'list' (singular), not 'names', so the verb is 'was'.
questions.tip: Find the head noun of the subject; ignore the 'of...' phrase.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling?
ms: 'I before e except after c' when the sound is 'ee': believe.
questions.tip: Learn ambitious words but spell them right. AO6 rewards accurate spelling of complex vocabulary.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the colon most effectively for a dramatic reveal?
options: There was: only one thing left in the room, a single red shoe.
There was only one thing: left in the room a single red shoe.
There: was only one thing left in the room a single red shoe.
There was only one thing left in the room: a single red shoe.
ms: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces what explains or reveals it.
questions.tip: The clause before a colon must be able to stand alone as a sentence.

questions.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? 'She walked ___ the room without speaking.'
ms: 'Past' is the preposition (beyond). 'Passed' is the past tense of the verb 'pass'.
questions.tip: Test: 'passed' is the past tense of the verb 'pass' ('she passed the ball'). If nothing is being passed, use 'past'.

questions.q:
Rewrite this extract with four errors corrected. Each correction is worth 1 mark.

'Their was no one left on the platform, I walked towards the exit. The train had went an hour ago. Everyone elses bags had gone too.'
questions.answer: There was no one left on the platform. I walked towards the exit. The train had gone an hour ago. Everyone else's bags had gone too.
ms: 1 mark: 'Their' corrected to 'There'
1 mark: comma splice corrected (full stop, semicolon, or 'so'/'and' after the comma)
1 mark: 'had went' corrected to 'had gone'
1 mark: 'elses' corrected to 'else's' (possessive apostrophe)
Accept any correct method of fixing the comma splice. Do not credit corrections that introduce new errors.
questions.tip: Most AO6 marks are lost on the same few errors: there/their, comma splices, verb forms, apostrophes.

questions.q: Write three sentences about a train arriving at a station that use: (a) a semicolon to link two related main clauses, (b) a pair of dashes for parenthesis, (c) a colon to introduce a list.
questions.answer:
(a) The train arrived ten minutes late; nobody on the platform seemed surprised.
(b) The driver - a tall woman with grey hair - leaned out of the cab and waved.
(c) Passengers poured out carrying everything imaginable: suitcases, pushchairs, bicycles and one enormous potted plant.
ms: 1 mark: (a) semicolon joins two complete, related main clauses with no conjunction
1 mark: (b) a pair of dashes encloses extra information that could be removed and leave a complete sentence
1 mark: (c) a colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list, correctly punctuated with commas
Do not credit a semicolon followed by a conjunction ('; and'), a single dash for parenthesis, or a colon after an incomplete clause ('carrying:').
questions.tip: Use each punctuation mark deliberately in Q5: a range of accurate punctuation is a Level 4 AO6 descriptor.

questions.q: Identify the technique: 'The kettle hissed and spat on the stove.'
ms: 'hissed' imitates sound (onomatopoeia) and 'spat' gives the kettle a human action (personification).
questions.tip: When two techniques overlap, name both and explain the combined effect.

questions.q: Identify the technique: 'Not a queue for the cafe, or the toilets, or the train.'
options: A tricolon (a list of three items)
ms: The negated list has three items ('the cafe, or the toilets, or the train'), a tricolon that builds comic disbelief before the reveal. It is not asyndeton, because the conjunction 'or' is present.
questions.tip: Asyndeton drops conjunctions (speed); polysyndeton repeats them between every item (weight); a tricolon is simply a list of three.

questions.q: Identify the technique: 'The children had the street, and the street had them.'
ms: Chiasmus repeats words in reverse order (A-B, B-A).
questions.tip: Chiasmus is rare, so spotting it impresses, but only if you explain how the reversal changes meaning.

questions.q: A writer lists a 'trowel', 'gloves', 'radio' and 'mug' in a dead man's glasshouse. Which term best describes the effect of grouping these words?
options: A semantic field of everyday life, emphasising how ordinary his routines were
ms: A semantic field is a group of words linked by topic; here they all belong to his daily life, which makes the absence sharper.
questions.tip: Name the field and explain what it builds: mood, theme or character.

questions.q: Which of these is an imperative sentence?
ms: An imperative gives a command. 'Breathe.' is a one-word imperative.
questions.tip: Imperatives in fiction can show a character talking to themselves; in non-fiction they direct the reader.

questions.q: Identify the technique: 'It is not freedom they need. It is someone to look after them.'
ms: Two parallel sentences set opposing ideas against each other: antithesis.
questions.tip: Antithesis is a strong ending device in Paper 2 Q5 too. Use it in your own conclusions.

questions.q: A story mentions early on that a cleaner is mopping the floor; at the end, the same cleaner hands the boy a letter. What is this technique called?
options: Foreshadowing / planting a detail that pays off later
ms: A detail planted early that becomes significant later is a structural setup.
questions.tip: In Q3, explain how a planted detail makes the ending feel surprising but inevitable.

questions.q: Which term describes a sentence that builds up details before reaching its main point, as in: 'And at the far end, in a cracked blue pot she had never seen before, something she did not recognise had opened a single flower'?
ms: The main clause ('something... had opened a single flower') is delayed by phrases, building suspense.
questions.tip: When you see delay, explain what the delay makes the reader feel: anticipation, suspense.

questions.q: Identify the technique: 'Breathe, she told herself. Breathe.'
ms: The word 'Breathe' is repeated for emphasis.
questions.tip: Explain the effect: here, repetition shows the first command did not work.

questions.q: Which term describes a writer's attitude towards their subject?
ms: Tone is the attitude shown through language; viewpoint (perspective) is the writer's opinion.
questions.tip: In Paper 2 Q3 and Q4, name the tone with a precise adjective and prove it with a quotation.

flashcards.back: 4 marks. About 5 minutes. List four explicit facts from the named lines only.

flashcards.front: P1 Q1: what does it test?
flashcards.back: AO1: identifying explicit (and sometimes implicit) information.
Using information from outside the named lines, or writing analysis. Short, true points only.
Yes. Short quotations or your own words both earn the mark, as long as the point is true.
1 hour 45 minutes. About 15 min reading, Q1 5, Q2 10, Q3 10, Q4 20, Q5 45.
80 marks: 40 reading (Section A), 40 writing (Section B). Worth 50% of the GCSE.
8 marks. About 10 minutes. Analyse language in a short given extract.

flashcards.front: P1 Q2: three things the bullets suggest
flashcards.back: Words and phrases; language features and techniques; sentence forms.
AO2: analyse how writers use language to achieve effects, using subject terminology.
Perceptive, detailed analysis; judicious short quotations; sophisticated terminology; explores layers of meaning.
'The verb ___ is particularly striking because it suggests...'
'On one level this suggests..., yet it could also imply...'
'The noun ___ carries connotations of..., which reinforces...'

flashcards.front: How many quotations for P1 Q2?
flashcards.back: About 3 to 4 short, well-chosen quotations explored in depth beats 8 skimmed ones.
8 marks. About 10 minutes. Covers the WHOLE source.
Beginning focus, shifts in focus as it develops, and the ending. Work through in order.
When the text moves attention, e.g. from setting to character, outside to inside, wide to close-up.

flashcards.front: Structure term: zoom in / narrowing focus
flashcards.back: The text moves from a wide view to one small detail, like a camera close-up.
Starting in the middle of the action, creating immediate tension or confusion.
A shift back in time to reveal backstory or explain a character's present.
Ending returns to an image or idea from the opening, often with a changed meaning.
Isolates a moment for emphasis, slows the pace or marks a turning point.
The moment the text changes direction, mood or focus, often signalled by 'But' or 'Then'.
An ending that leaves a question unanswered to create suspense.
Delaying a key detail to build suspense and curiosity.
Introducing speech can break a descriptive section, introduce a new character or shift the pace.
'At the start, the writer focuses the reader's attention on..., which establishes...'
'The focus then shifts to..., which creates a sense of...'
'By ending with..., the writer leaves the reader feeling...'
20 marks. About 20 minutes. The biggest reading question on Paper 1.
AO4: evaluate texts critically, with appropriate textual references.

flashcards.front: P1 Q4: what does 'to what extent' want?
flashcards.back: A clear judgement: agree, mostly agree or partly agree, explained with evidence.

flashcards.front: P1 Q4: three things to cover
flashcards.back: Your impressions; how the writer creates them (methods); evidence from the text.
'The writer is most successful in conveying ___ when...'
'I largely agree, although the word ___ in the statement is perhaps too strong because...'
Critical, convincing, detailed; perceptive about methods; judicious quotations; argues rather than describes.

flashcards.front: P1 Q4: can you use structure as well as language?
flashcards.back: Yes. Any method counts: language, structure, characterisation, setting.
40 marks: 24 content and organisation (AO5) + 16 technical accuracy (AO6). About 45 minutes.
Usually a choice: describe a picture, or write a story/description from a prompt. Only answer one.
Plan 5 min, write 35 min, proofread 5 min.

flashcards.front: Descriptive structure: drop, shift, zoom, flash, echo
flashcards.back: Drop into a scene; shift focus; zoom into a detail; flash back or forward; echo the opening at the end.
One setting, one or two characters, one key moment. Less plot means more crafting.
Plan the ending before starting. A quiet, resonant ending beats 'it was all a dream'.
Content and organisation: tone, register, vocabulary, crafted devices, structural features, paragraphing.
Not 'She was nervous' but 'She twisted the ring on her finger until the skin beneath it burned.'
Description lingers on a moment with little plot. Narrative has characters, events and change.
Crafted structure; ambitious, precise vocabulary; sentences varied for effect; near-flawless SPaG.
4 marks. About 5 minutes. Shade four TRUE statements from eight.

flashcards.front: P2 Q1: what if you shade five?
flashcards.back: Don't. The question says 'choose a maximum of four'. Shade exactly four and check each against the named lines.
They change one detail: a number, a time, 'all' for 'some', or a feeling the writer never states.
1 hour 45 minutes. About 15 min reading, Q1 5, Q2 8, Q3 12, Q4 20, Q5 45.
Two non-fiction texts: usually one 19th century and one 20th or 21st century, linked by topic.
8 marks. About 8 minutes. Summarise differences using both sources.
AO1: synthesise evidence and make inferences from different texts.

flashcards.front: P2 Q2: what NOT to do
flashcards.back: Analyse language techniques. Q2 rewards what the texts say and imply, not how they are written.
Whereas, however, by contrast, on the other hand, conversely, unlike.
'This implies that...' / 'This suggests the writer...'
Similarly, likewise, equally, in the same way, both writers.
12 marks. About 12 minutes. Language analysis on ONE source only.
P2 Q3 is worth 12, not 8, and uses non-fiction. Explore tone and the writer's attitude.
Sardonic, wry, indignant, nostalgic, condescending, earnest, scathing, reverent, ambivalent.
'The writer's tone here is ___, conveyed through...'
16 marks. About 20 minutes. Compare perspectives AND methods across both whole sources.
AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how they are conveyed.
Perspective A vs B, method A vs B with quotations, effect, reason for difference (context, purpose).
'While Writer A sees ___ as..., Writer B presents it as...'
Briefly explain why perspectives differ (era, purpose, audience). Never write a history essay.
Perspective = the writer's attitude or viewpoint. Method = how they convey it (language, tone, structure).
40 marks: 24 AO5 + 16 AO6. About 45 minutes. Write to argue, persuade, explain or advise.
Genre/form, Audience, Purpose. Match your register to all three.
Address, salutation ('Dear...'), formal paragraphs, sign-off ('Yours sincerely' named / 'Yours faithfully' unnamed).
Headline, optional subheading or strapline, paragraphs, engaging opening.
Direct address to audience ('Good morning, everyone'), spoken features, rhetorical questions, memorable ending.
Acknowledging and rebutting the other side shows sophistication and makes your argument stronger.
Ethos = credibility; pathos = emotion; logos = logic and evidence.
A group of three for rhythm and emphasis: 'safer, healthier and happier'.
A short personal story to make an argument relatable and emotional.
Asking a question and then answering it: 'Why does this matter? Because...'
Return to the opening image or hook, then end with a clear call to action.
Agree with the problem but challenge the solution. Reads as more mature than total agreement.
Two main clauses joined only by a comma. Fix with a full stop, semicolon or conjunction.
Joins two related main clauses; or separates list items that already contain commas.
After a complete clause, to introduce a list, an explanation or a dramatic reveal.
Shows missing letters: do not = don't, it is = it's, they are = they're.
Add 's: the girl's bag, James's coat.
Plural ending in s: add ' (the girls' bags). Irregular: add 's (children's, women's).
Its = belonging to it. It's = it is / it has.
Affect = verb (to influence). Effect = noun (the result).
Practice = noun. Practise = verb. Same for licence / license, advice / advise.
Lose = misplace or fail to win. Loose = not tight.
Then = time. Than = comparison.
One main clause: 'The door creaked.'
Two main clauses joined by FANBOYS: 'The door creaked, and the lights failed.'
A main clause plus a subordinate clause: 'As the door creaked, the lights failed.'
A deliberate fragment without a main verb, for effect: 'Darkness.'
Extra information inserted with commas, brackets or dashes: 'My aunt, a nurse, works nights.'
'I'm leaving,' she said. Punctuation inside the speech marks; new line for each new speaker.
Shows a trailing off, pause or omission. Use once at most in a piece; overuse looks careless.
One collar (c), two sleeves (ss): necessary.
There is 'a rat' in separate.
Contains 'finite': de-finite-ly.
Double r, double s: embarrass.
Beginning (double n), occurred (double c, double r), recommend (one c, double m).
An adverb or phrase starting a sentence, followed by a comma: 'Without warning, the ground shook.'
Range of vocabulary and sentence structures, and accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar.
Comparison using 'like' or 'as': 'The fog clung like wet wool.'
Says one thing IS another: 'The classroom was a zoo.'
A metaphor developed across several lines or a whole text.
Giving human qualities to a non-human thing: 'The wind howled its grief.'
Weather or setting reflecting emotion: storm clouds before a tragedy.
Repeated initial consonant sounds: 'bitter, biting breeze'.
Repeated 's' or 'sh' sounds, often sinister or soothing: 'silent, slithering shadows'.
Harsh 'b', 'p', 't', 'd', 'k' sounds that suggest anger or violence.
Repeated vowel sounds: 'the low moan of the cold road'.
A word that imitates its sound: crash, hiss, thud.
Two contradictory words together: 'deafening silence'.
Placing contrasting ideas side by side to highlight difference.
Contrasting ideas in a balanced structure: 'Not a privilege for the few, but an expectation for all.'
Deliberate exaggeration: 'I waited a lifetime for that bus.'
Understatement using a negative: 'not bad at all' meaning very good.
Repeating words at the start of successive clauses: 'I remember... I remember...'
A list without conjunctions: speeds up, piles on. 'Rain, wind, hail, thunder.'
A list with repeated conjunctions: slows, overwhelms. 'wide and brown and generous'.
A group of words linked by topic: 'mourners, grave, black' create a field of death.
The associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning: 'blood-red' suggests violence.
A command verb: 'Act now.' Creates urgency in persuasive writing.
Speaking to the reader as 'you' to create involvement.
Words chosen to provoke strong feeling: 'helpless', 'devastated'.
A comic drop from serious to trivial: 'He lost his home, his job and his umbrella.'
Saying the opposite of what is meant, or an outcome opposite to what is expected.
A softened phrase for something unpleasant: 'passed away'.
A recurring image or idea, e.g. clocks repeated to suggest time running out.
An early hint at what will come later.

flashcards.front: Word classes to name in analysis
flashcards.back: Noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition, conjunction. 'The verb ___' is precise terminology.
Show certainty or possibility: must, will, should, might, could. 'Must' = certainty; 'might' = tentative.
Luminous, iridescent, incandescent, flickering, gleaming, spectral.
Sombre, murky, shadowed, oppressive, stygian, crepuscular (twilight).
Cacophony, reverberate, muffled, shrill, guttural, susurrus (soft rustling).
Dilapidated, derelict, corroded, crumbling, desolate, forsaken.
Apprehensive, melancholy, elated, forlorn, resolute, trepidation.
Undeniable, indefensible, crucial, detrimental, imperative, unprecedented.
Firstly, furthermore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, ultimately.

flashcards.front: P2 Q1: how many statements are there?
flashcards.back: Eight statements (A to H). Four are true, four are false.

flashcards.front: P2 Q1: which part of the source?
flashcards.back: Only the lines named (usually the first few paragraphs of Source A). Ignore everything else.
AO1: identify and interpret explicit and implicit information.
Check every number and time against the text: 'eleven' vs 'twelve', 'sixteen a penny' vs 'twelve'.
Watch for 'all', 'always', 'never', 'only', 'every'. A statement with 'only' is false if the text says 'many'.
A statement that gives the writer a feeling or opinion they never state is false, even if it seems likely.
Some true statements are implied, not word-for-word. True if the text clearly supports it, e.g. 'nobody talks much' supports 'the queue is quiet'.
Read the statement, find the matching line, underline the key word, mark T or F. Do all eight before shading.
Distractors often swap who did what (the lads filmed themselves, not the writer). Check who the subject is.
If Q1 is on an older text, slow down: long sentences and old words ('twelvemonth' = a year) hide the detail.
A statement can combine two facts (40 minutes + 5 more = 45). Both halves must be true.

flashcards.front: P2 Q1: what if you change your mind?
flashcards.back: Cross out clearly. The instruction is 'choose a maximum of four', so make sure the final four shaded boxes are obvious.
4 near-certain marks in 5 minutes. Rushing it to get to Q2 is the worst trade on the paper.
Judge only what the writer says, not what is true in real life or what you think.
The question names a focus (people, places, experiences). Only use details that fit that focus.
Difference + quotation from A + inference + connective + quotation from B + inference.
Two or three well-developed differences beat five thin ones. About 8 minutes in total.
Bringing details from both sources together into one point, not writing about each separately.
Implies, suggests, reveals, indicates, hints, conveys that...
Go one step further than the obvious: not just 'she is poor' but 'every penny decides what the family eats on Sunday'.
Embed one to four words: the woman counted her coins 'three times'. Long quotations waste time.

flashcards.front: P2 Q2: difference inside a similarity
flashcards.back: 'While both writers feel better after the cold, A seeks it deliberately, whereas B is surprised by it.' A Level 4 move.

flashcards.front: P2 Q2: is it always differences?
flashcards.back: Usually, but read the question: it may ask for similarities. Answer exactly what is asked.

flashcards.front: P2 Q2: can you mention context?
flashcards.back: Only to explain an inference briefly. Do not write about historical background for its own sake.
Q2 = WHAT is different (content, 8 marks, AO1). Q4 = perspectives AND methods (16 marks, AO3).
Paraphrase without inference ('A is busy, B is quiet') stays at Level 2.
Start with an overview: 'The children in Source A are protected to the point of anxiety, whereas those in Source B are left almost wholly unguarded.'
AO2: analyse how writers use language to achieve effects, using subject terminology.
Only the source named, which is Source B in AQA papers. Writing about the other source scores nothing.
Often a section or the whole of one source, so choose the 4-6 richest quotations across it.
Map how the tone shifts (amused, then concerned, then hopeful) and analyse the words that create each shift.

flashcards.front: P2 Q3: non-fiction devices to spot
flashcards.back: Statistics, anecdote, direct address, rhetorical questions, irony, hyperbole, antithesis, lists, imperatives.
Look for formal lexis, long balanced sentences, moral language ('respectable', 'wicked') and direct appeals to the reader.
Look for informal register, humour, colloquialisms, short sentences and parenthetical asides.
Colons, dashes and parentheses count as language. Explain the effect: a colon before 'awake' isolates a revelation.
Always link effects back to the writer's viewpoint: what does this word reveal about how they feel?
Building up then dropping to something trivial ('an inflatable flamingo'). Creates comedy; often makes a serious point.
Saying one thing but meaning another ('respectable people' used critically). Name it and explain the criticism.
'The adverb "tenderly" transforms money into something precious, suggesting...'
Never write 'the writer uses alliteration to make it interesting'. Name, quote, explain the precise effect.
Three or four analytical paragraphs in about 12 minutes, each zooming into one or two quotations.
Use the whole of BOTH sources, not just the opening paragraphs.
One sentence on both writers' views: 'Both admire children's spirit, but the modern parent wants more freedom while the Victorian journalist wants more care.'

flashcards.front: P2 Q4: what counts as a method?
flashcards.back: Language, tone, structure, form (letter, article), evidence (statistics, anecdote), voice, endings.
Compare openings and endings: how each writer begins and where they leave the reader.
Private letter = confiding, informal; newspaper article = public, persuasive; travel book = personal reflection.
Name each writer's tone with a precise adjective: wry vs indignant, ambivalent vs certain.
Explain how what each writer wants (to persuade, entertain, inform) shapes their methods.
Find a hidden link: both use balanced aphorisms, but to reach opposite conclusions.
Three or four comparative paragraphs. Every paragraph covers both sources.
Whereas, by contrast, similarly, both writers, unlike, while... on the other hand.

flashcards.front: P2 Q4: why do views differ?
flashcards.back: Era (what was normal then), purpose, audience, personal experience. One sentence, linked to evidence.
Writing all about A, then all about B. Even with good analysis, no integration caps the mark.
Optional. If you write one, make it a perceptive final judgement in one or two sentences.
An opening wide view of a setting before focusing on a character, like a film camera.
Moving from the wide setting to small details or one character, which builds intensity.
Pulling back from a detail to the wider world, often to show isolation or scale.
The speed of the narrative. Short sentences and paragraphs slow time at tense moments; summary speeds it up.
An early detail that becomes important later (the cleaner, the label). Makes endings feel inevitable.
Establishing a normal pattern ('Each afternoon at four') so a change stands out.
A change in whose point of view or gaze we follow ('Then he looked at hers').
Phrases like 'At twenty past four... At half past' that control pace and build anticipation.
A repeated image (the small pool) that returns changed, showing a character's development.
An ending that leaves the outcome unresolved, making the reader wonder what happens next.
Beginning (what we focus on and why), middle (the shift and why), end (how it leaves us and why).
Structure = where and when things appear in the text. A simile is language unless you explain why it is placed where it is.
Balanced opposites: 'not a nuisance but a necessity'. Memorable endings and topic sentences.
A question for effect that makes the reader agree in their head: 'Who was the first face you saw today?'
Use plausible, general figures ('hundreds of thousands') or rounded ones. Never claim a precise invented source as real.
'Studies suggest...' / 'Doctors warn...' adds ethos. Keep it general and believable.
'You' pulls the reader in and makes the issue personal.
'We' and 'us' create unity between writer and reader: 'If we want...'
'Of course, critics are right that...' then turn with 'but'. Makes you sound fair and reasonable.
A short, specific story (a pacing polar bear, colouring a map at 11pm) that brings the argument to life.
Self-deprecating humour builds trust in articles and speeches. Avoid sarcasm in formal letters.

flashcards.front: Persuasive device: short sentence for impact
flashcards.back: After a long argument, a short sentence lands the point: 'It is not cheap.'
A command for a call to action: 'Write to your councillor today.'
Return to the opening anecdote or image, changed by your argument. Very effective in Q5.
Title, introduction with a thesis, topic sentences, counter-argument, conclusion. Formal, reasoned voice.

flashcards.front: P2 Q5: argue vs persuade vs explain
flashcards.back: Argue = reasoned case, often with counter-argument; persuade = emotional push to act; explain = measured reasons for a view.
15 min reading, Q1 5 min, Q2 10 min, Q3 10 min, Q4 20 min. About 1 hour in total.
45 minutes for Q5: about 5-10 plan, 30-35 write, 5 proofread.
45 minutes for Q5: plan the stance, counter-argument and ending first.
1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks: Section A reading 40, Section B writing 40.
About one minute per mark on reading questions. Q4 on Paper 1 = 20 marks = about 20 minutes.
About 12 minutes. Do not let it eat into Q4 (16 marks) or Q5 (40 marks).
About 8 minutes. Three linked differences is enough.
About 20 minutes. Leave the full 45 minutes for Q5 afterwards.
About 10 minutes. Three paragraphs, each zooming into one quotation.
About 10 minutes. Beginning, middle, end: three paragraphs.
Test both halves ('hopeful AND painful'). The best answers show how one detail creates both.
Challenge a strong word in the statement ('completely', 'clear') to show critical judgement.
Convincingly, powerfully, subtly, most effectively, partly, arguably, ultimately.
State your judgement in sentence one: 'I largely agree, but...'

flashcards.front: P1 Q2: sentence forms to name
flashcards.back: Minor sentence (fragment), simple, compound, complex, cumulative, imperative, exclamatory, interrogative.

flashcards.front: P1 Q2: zoom-in on one word
flashcards.back: 'The verb "crawling" suggests slow, laborious effort, as if the bus is struggling against the mountain itself.'
Allowed if clearly supported by the text. Safer to stick to explicit facts.
The question says 'about X'. Every point must be about X, not something nearby.
You do not have to describe everything in the picture. Pick details and build a shape around them.
Copy it exactly as your first sentence, then make the second sentence do real work.

flashcards.front: P1 Q5: 'opening part of a story'
flashcards.back: You do not need to finish the plot. End on a hook or choice that makes the reader want more.
A recurring object or image (a key, earphones, light) that ties the piece together and returns changed at the end.
Words repeated in reverse order: 'The children had the street, and the street had them.'
A sentence that delays its main clause with phrases, building suspense before the key idea.
Exaggerated description of a person for comic effect: 'a face as red as a boiled ham'.
Two main clauses with no punctuation: 'The bus was late I missed it.' Fix with full stop, semicolon or comma + conjunction.
Who's = who is / who has. Whose = belonging to whom.
Passed = verb (she passed the test). Past = preposition or noun (she walked past; in the past).
